The dam is generally hydrologically significant if it is: 1. 25 feet or more in height from the natural bed of the stream and has a storage of at least 15 acre-feet. 2. Or has an impounding capacity of 50 acre-feet or more and is at least six feet above the natural bed of the stream.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DAMBRK is: In hydrologic terms, the Dam Break Forecasting Model.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DAPM is: In hydrologic terms, the Data Acquisition Program Manager.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dark Surge on Disk (DSD) is: In solar-terrestrial terms, dark gaseous ejections visible in H-alpha.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dart Leader is: A faint, negatively charged channel that travels more or less directly and continuously from cloud to ground.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Data Point is: In the context of hydrologic observations, a location on a river/stream for which observed data is input to RFC or WFO hydrologic forecast procedures, or included in public hydroÂ­logic products. Flood forecasts and warnings are not issued for data points (see /forecast point/).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DATACOL is: In hydrologic terms, the Software System that supports RFC gateway functions.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DATANET is: In hydrologic terms, it is the hydrologic Data Network Analysis Software.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dawn is: Same as Civil Dawn ; the time of morning at which the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. At this time, there is enough light for objects to be distiguishable and that outdoor activities can commence.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Day Length is: Duration of the period from sunrise to sunset.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, dBZ is: Nondimensional "unit" of radar reflectivity which represents a logarithmic power ratio (in decibels, or dB) with respect to radar reflectivity factor, Z.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DCP is: (Data Collection Platform) In hydrologic terms, an electronic device that connects to a river or rainfall gage that records data from the gage and at pre-determined times transmits that data through a satellite to a remote computer.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DDS is: Data Distribution System.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dead Storage is: In hydrologic terms, the volume in a reservoir below the lowest controllable level.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Debris Cloud is: A rotating "cloud" of dust or debris, near or on the ground, often appearing beneath a condensation funnel and surrounding the base of a tornado. This term is similar to dust whirl, although the latter typically refers to a circulation which contains dust but not necessarily any debris. A dust plume, on the other hand, does not rotate. Note that a debris cloud appearing beneath a thunderstorm will confirm the presence of a tornado, even in the absence of a condensation funnel.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Decadal is: Occurring over a 10-year period, such as an oscillation whose period is roughly 10 years ("Pacific Decadal Oscillation").

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Declination is: The latitude that the sun is directly over at a given time. The declination is ~23Â°N at the summer solstice, ~23Â°S at the winter solstice, and 0Â° (over the equator) at the spring and autumn equinoxes.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deep Percolation Loss is: In hydrologic terms, water that percolates downward through the soil beyond the reach of plant roots.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deep Seepage is: In hydrologic terms, infiltration which reaches the water table.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deep well is: In hydrologic terms, a well whose pumping head is too great to permit use of a suction pump.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deepening is: A decrease in the central pressure of a surface low pressure system. The storm is intensifying.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deformation Zone is: The change in shape of a fluid mass by variations in wind, specifically by stretching and/or shearing. Deformation is a primary factor in frontogenesis (evolution of fronts) and frontolysis (decay of fronts).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Deformed Ice is: In hydrologic terms, a general term for ice which has been squeezed together and forced upwards and downwards in places. Subdivisions are rated ice, ridge ice, hummocked ice, and other similar deformations.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Degradation is: In hydrologic terms, the geologic process by means of which various parts of the surface of the earth are worn down and carried away and their general level lowered, by the action of wind and water.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Degree Day is: A measure that gauges the amount of heating or cooling needed for a building using 65 degrees as a baseline. Electrical, natural gas, power, and heating, and air conditioning industries utilize heating and cooling degree information to calculate their needs. For more specific definitions and how to calculate degree days, see the definitions for Heating Degree Days and Cooling Degree Days .

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Delta T is: Change in temperature. 1) A simple representation of the mean lapse rate within a layer of the atmosphere, obtained by calculating the difference between observed temperatures at the bottom and top of the layer. Delta Ts often are computed operationally over the layer between pressure levels of 700 mb and 500 mb, in order to evaluate the amount of instability in mid-levels of the atmosphere. Generally, values greater than about 18 indicate sufficient instability for severe thunderstorm development. 2) The difference in temperature between the surface of a lake and 850mb, typically used to determine lake effect snow potential.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Delta is: In hydrologic terms, an alluvial deposit, often in the shape of the Greek letter "delta", which is formed where a stream drops its debris load on entering a body of quieter water.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dendrites is: In hydrologic terms, thin branch-like growth of ice on the water surface.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dendritic is: In hydrologic terms, the form of the drainage pattern of a stream and it's tributaries when it follows a treelike shape, with the main trunk, branches, and twigs corresponding to the main stream, tributaries, and subtributaries, respectively, of the stream.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dense Fog Advisory is: This product is issued when fog reduces visibility to 1/4 mile or less over a widespread area. For marine products: an advisory for widespread or localized fog reducing visibilities to regionally or locally defined limitations not to exceed 1 nautical mile.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dense Smoke Advisory is: This product is issued for widespread or localized smoke reducing visibilities to ¼ mile or less.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Density Current is: In hydrologic terms, a flow of water maintained by gravity through a large body of water, such as a reservoir or lake, and retaining its unmixed identity because of a difference in density.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Density of Snow is: In hydrologic terms, the ratio, expressed as a percentage, of the volume which a given quantity of snow would occupy if it were reduced to water, to the volume of the snow. When a snow sampler is used, it is the ratio expressed as percentage of the scale reading on the sampler to the length of the snow core or sample.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Depletion Curve is: In hydrologic terms, the part of the hydrograph extending from the point of termination of the Recession Curve to the subsequent rise or alternation of inflow due to additional water becomming available for stream flow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Depression Storage is: In hydrologic terms, the volume of water contained in natural depressions in the land surface, such as puddles.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Depression is: A region of low atmospheric pressure that is usually accompanied by low clouds and precipitation. The term is also sometimes used as a reference to a Tropical Depression.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Depth of Runoff is: In hydrologic terms, the total runoff from a drainage basin, divided by its area. For convenience in comparing runoff with precipitation, the term is usually expressed in inches of depth during a given period of time over the drainage area or acre-feet per square mile.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Derecho is: (Pronounced day-RAY-cho), a widespread and usually fast-moving windstorm associated with convection. Derechos include any family of downburst clusters produced by an extratropical MCS, and can produce damaging straight-line winds over areas hundreds of miles long and more than 100 miles across.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Derived Products is: Processed base data on the Doppler radar.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Desertification is: A tendency toward more prominent desert conditions in a region.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Design Criteria is: In hydrologic terms, the hypothetical flood used in the sizing of the dam and the associated structures to prevent dam failure by overtopping, especially for the spillway and outlet works.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Detention Basins is: Structures built upstream from populated areas to prevent runoff and/or debris flows from causing property damage and loss of life. They are normally dry, but are designed to attenuate storm flows or detain mud/debris during and immediately after a runoff event. They have no spillway gates or valves and do not store water on a long-term basis. Typical detention times for storm flows are on the order of 24 to 72 hours, but may be as long as 5 to 10 days. Basins designed for detention of mud and rock debris are periodically excavated to maintain their storage capacity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Detention Storage is: In hydrologic terms, the volume of water, other than depression storage, existing on the land surface as flowing water which has not yet reached the channel.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Detritus is: In hydrologic terms, (1) the heavier mineral debris moved by natural watercourses, usually in bed-load form. (2) the sand, grit, and other coarse material removed by differential sedimentation in a relatively short period of detention.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Developing Gale/Storm is: In the high seas and offshore forecasts, a headline used in the warnings section to indicate that gale/storm force winds are not now occurring but are expected before the end of the forecast period.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dew Point Depression is: The difference in degrees between the air temperature and the dew point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dew Point Front is: A narrow zone (mesoscale feature) of extremely sharp moisture gradient and little temperature gradient. It separates moist air from dry air. Severe weather can be associated with this front. It is also known as a "dryline" or "dry front".

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dew Point is: (Abbrev. DWPT) - A measure of atmospheric moisture. It is the temperature to which air must be cooled in order to reach saturation (assuming air pressure and moisture content are constant). A higher dew point indicates more moisture present in the air. It is sometimes referred to as Dew Point Temperature, and sometimes written as one word (Dewpoint).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dew is: Moisture that has condensed on objects near the ground, whose temperatures have fallen below the dewpoint temperature.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DEWP is: On a buoy report, the dewpoint temperature taken at the same height as the air temperature measurement.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diabatic is: A process which occurs with the addition or loss of heat. The opposite of adiabatic. Meteorological examples include air parcels warming due to the absorption of infrared radiation or release of latent heat.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diablo Wind is: Similar to Santa Ana winds in southern California. These winds occur below canyons in the East Bay hills (Diablo range) and in extreme cases can exceed 60 mph. They develop due to high pressure over Nevada and lower pressure along the central California coast.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diagnostic Model is: A computer model used to calculate air pollution concentrations. A diagnostic model produces a wind field over an area by interpolating from actual wind observations.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diamond Dust is: A fall of non-branched (snow crystals are branched) ice crystals in the form of needles, columns, or plates.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Differential Motion is: Cloud motion that appears to differ relative to other nearby cloud elements, e.g. clouds moving from left to right relative to other clouds in the foreground or background. Cloud rotation is one example of differential motion, but not all differential motion indicates rotation. For example, horizontal wind shear along a gust front may result in differential cloud motion without the presence of rotation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Differential Rotation is: In solar-terrestrial terms, the change in solar rotation rate with latitude. Low latitudes rotate at a faster angular rate (approx. 14 degrees per day) than do high latitudes (approx. 12 degrees per day).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diffuse Ice is: In hydrologic terms, poorly defined ice edge limiting an area of dispersed ice; usually on the leeward side of an area of floating ice.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Difluence is: (or diffluence) - A pattern of wind flow in which air moves outward (in a "fan-out" pattern) away from a central axis that is oriented parallel to the general direction of the flow. It is the opposite of confluence. Difluence in an upper level wind field is considered a favorable condition for severe thunderstorm development (if other parameters are also favorable). But difluence is not the same as divergence. In a difluent flow, winds normally decelerate as they move through the region of difluence, resulting in speed convergence which offsets the apparent diverging effect of the difluent flow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DIR is: 1. Direction 2. On a buoy report, the ten-minute average wind direction measurements in degrees clockwise from true North.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Direct Flood Damage is: In hydrologic terms, the damage done to property, structures, goods, etc., by a flood as measured by the cost of replacement and repairs.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Direct Hit is: A close approach of a tropical cyclone to a particular location. For locations on the left-hand side of a tropical cyclone's track (looking in the direction of motion), a direct hit occurs when the cyclone passes to within a distance equal to the cyclone's radius of maximum wind. For locations on the right-hand side of the track, a direct hit occurs when the cyclone passes to within a distance equal to twice the radius of maximum wind. Compare indirect hit, strike.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Direct Runoff is: In hydrologic terms, the runoff entering stream channels promptly after rainfall or snowmelt. Superposed on base runoff, it forms the bulk of the hydrograph of a flood.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Direct Solar Radiation is: The component of solar radiation received by the earth's surface only from the direction of the sun's disk (i.e. it has not been reflected, refracted or scattered).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Directional Shear is: The component of wind shear which is due to a change in wind direction with height, e.g., southeasterly winds at the surface and southwesterly winds aloft. A veering wind with height in the lower part of the atmosphere is a type of directional shear often considered important for tornado development.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Disappearing Solar Filament (DSF) is: In solar-terrestrial terms, the sudden (timescale of minutes to hours) disappearance of a solar filament (prominence).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Discharge Curve is: In hydrologic terms, a curve that expresses the relation between the discharge of a stream or open conduit at a given location and the stage or elevation of the liquid surface at or near that location. Also called Rating Curve and Discharge Rating Curve.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Discharge Table is: In hydrologic terms, 1. A table showing the relation between two mutually dependant quantities or variable over a given range of magnitude. 2. A table showing the relation between the gage height and the discharge of a stream or conduit at a given gaging station. Also called a Rating Table.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Discharge is: In hydrologic terms, the rate at which water passes a given point. Discharge is expressed in a volume per time with units of L 3 /T. Discharge is often used interchangeably with streamflow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Disdrometer is: Equipment that measures and records the size distribution of raindrops.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Disk is: The visible surface of the sun (or any heavenly body) projected against the sky.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dispersion is: The process of separating radiation into various wavelengths.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Distribution (Hydro)Graph is: In hydrologic terms, a unit hydrograph of direct runoff modified to show the proportions of the volume of runoff that occur during successive equal units of time.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diurnal Cycles is: Variations in meteorological parameters such as temperature and relative humidity over the course of a day which result from the rotation of the Earth about its axis and the resultant change in incoming and outgoing radiation.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diurnal Temperature Range is: The temperature difference between the minimum at night (low) and the maximum during the day (high).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diurnal is: Daily; related to actions which are completed in the course of a calendar day, and which typically recur every calendar day (e.g., diurnal temperature rises during the day, and diurnal falls at night).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Divergence is: The expansion or spreading out of a vector field; usually said of horizontal winds. It is the opposite of convergence. Divergence at upper levels of the atmosphere enhances upward motion, and hence the potential for thunderstorm development (if other factors also are favorable).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Diversion is: In hydrologic terms, the taking of water from a stream or other body of water into a canal, pipe, or other conduit.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Divide is: In hydrologic terms, the high ground that forms the boundary of a watershed. A divide is also called a ridge.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dividing Streamline Height is: The height above ground of the dividing streamline, as measured far upwind of a mountain barrier. See dividing streamline.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dividing Streamline is: In the blocked flow region upwind of a mountain barrier, the streamline that separates the blocked flow region near the ground from the streamlines above which go over the barrier.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DNR is: Department of Natural Resources

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dobson Unit is: Unit used to measure the abundance of ozone in the atmosphere. One Dobson unit is the equivalent of 2.69/ x 10 16 molecules of ozone/cm 2 .
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DOC is: Department of Commerce
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DOH is: Development and Operations Hydrologist
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Doldrums is: The regions on either side of the equator where air pressure is low and winds are light.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Domain is: In air pollution modeling, the geographical area over which a simulation is performed.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Domestic Consumption is: In hydrologic terms, the quantity, or quantity per capita, of water consumed in a municipality or district for domestic uses or purposes during a given period, generally one day. It is usually taken to include all uses included within the term Municipal Use of Water and quantity wasted, lost, or otherwise unaccounted for.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Domestic Use of water is: In hydrologic terms, the use of water primarily for household purposes, the watering of livestock, the irrigation of gardens, lawns, shrubbery, etc., surrounding a house or domicile.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Doppler Radar is: Radar that can measure radial velocity, the instantaneous component of motion parallel to the radar beam (i.e., toward or away from the radar antenna).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Down-Valley Wind is: A thermally driven wind directed down a valley's axis, usually occurring during nighttime; part of the along-valley wind system.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downburst is: A strong downdraft current of air from a cumulonimbus cloud, often associated with intense thunderstorms. Downdrafts may produce damaging winds at the surface.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downdraft is: (Abbrev. DWNDFT) - A small-scale column of air that rapidly sinks toward the ground, usually accompanied by precipitation as in a shower or thunderstorm. A downburst is the result of a strong downdraft.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downslope Flow is: A thermally driven wind directed down a mountain slope and usually occurring at night; part of the along-slope wind system.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downstream Slope is: In hydrologic terms, the slope or face of the dam away from the reservoir water. This slope requires some kind of protection (e.g.; grass) from the erosive effects of rain and surface flow
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downstream is: In the same direction as a stream or other flow, or toward the direction in which the flow is moving.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downwash is: A deflection of air downward relative to an object that causes the deflection.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Downwelling Radiation is: The component of radiation directed toward the earth's surface from the sun or the atmosphere, opposite of upwelling radiation.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DP is: 1. Deep 2. Dew Point
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DPD is: On a buoy report, dominant wave period (seconds) is the period with the maximum wave energy.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DPVA is: Differential Positive Vorticity Advection
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drainage Area is: In hydrologic terms, an area having a common outlet for its surface runoff (also see Watershed and Catchment Area).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drainage Basin is: In hydrologic terms, a part of the surface of the earth that is occupied by a drainage system, which consists of a surface stream or a body of impounded surface water together with all tributary surface streams and bodies of impounded surface water.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drainage Density is: In hydrologic terms, the relative density of natural drainage channels in a given area. It is usually expressed in terms of miles of natural drainage or stream channel per square mile of area, and obtained by dividing the total length of stream channels in the area in miles by the area in square miles.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drainage Divide is: In hydrologic terms, the boundary line, along a topographic ridge or along a subsurface formation, separating two adjacent drainage basins.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drainer is: A valley or basin from which air drains continuously during nighttime rather than becoming trapped or pooled.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drains (Relief Wells) is: In hydrologic terms, a vertical well or borehole, usually downstream of impervious cores, grout curtains or cutoffs, designed to collect and direct seepage through or under a dam to reduce uplift pressure under or within a dam. A line of such wells forms a "drainage curtain".

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drawdown is: In hydrologic terms, the lowering of the surface elevation of a body of water, the water surface of a well, the water table, or the piezometric surface adjacent to the well, resulting from the withdrawl of water therefrom.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dredging is: In hydrologic terms, the scooping, or suction of underwater material from a harbor, or waterway. Dredging is one form of channel modification. It is often too expensive to be practical because the dredged material must be disposed of somewhere and the stream will usually fill back up with sediment in a few years. Dredging is usually undertaken only on large rivers to maintain a navigation channel.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drifting Ice is: In hydrologic terms, pieces of floating ice moving under the action of wind and/ or currents.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drifting Snow is: Drifting snow is an uneven distribution of snowfall/snow depth caused by strong surface winds. Drifting snow may occur during or after a snowfall. Drifting snow is usually associated with blowing snow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drizzle is: Precipitation consisting of numerous minute droplets of water less than 0.5 mm (500 micrometers) in diameter.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drop-size Distribution is: The distribution of rain drops or cloud droplets of specified sizes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drought Assessments is: At the end of each month, CPC issues a long-term seasonal drought assessment. On Thursdays of each week, the CPC together with NOAA National Climatic Data Center, the United States Department of Agriculture, and the National Drought Mitigation Center in Lincoln, Nebraska, issues a weekly drought assessment called the United States Drought Monitor. These assessments review national drought conditions and indicate potential impacts for various economic sectors, such as agriculture and forestry.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drought Index is: In hydrologic terms, computed value which is related to some of the cumulative effects of a prolonged and abnormal moisture deficiency. (An index of hydrological drought corresponding to levels below the mean in streams, lakes, and reservoirs.)

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Drought is: Drought is a deficiency of moisture that results in adverse impacts on people, animals, or vegetation over a sizeable area. NOAA together with its partners provides short- and long-term Drought Assessments.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Adiabat is: A line of constant potential temperature on a thermodynamic chart.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate is: The rate at which the temperature of a parcel of dry air decreases as the parcel is lifted in the atmosphere. The dry adiabatic lapse rate (abbreviated DALR) is 5.5Â°F per 1000 ft or 9.8Â°C per km.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry-adiabatic is: 1. An adiabatic process in a hypothetical atmosphere in which no moisture is present. 2. An adiabatic process in which no condensation of its water vapor occurs and no liquid water is present.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Crack is: In hydrologic terms, a crack visible at the surface but not going right through the ice cover, and therefore it is dry.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Floodproofing is: In hydrologic terms, a dry floodproofed building is sealed against floodwaters. All areas below the flood protection level are made watertight. Walls are coated with waterproofing compounds or plastic sheeting. Openings like doors windows, sewer lines and vents are closed, whether permanently, with removable shields, or with sandbags. The flood protection level should be no more than 2 or 3 feet above the top of the foundation because the buildings walls and floors cannot withstand the pressure of deeper water.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Line Bulge is: A bulge in the dry line, representing the area where dry air is advancing most strongly at lower levels. Severe weather potential is increased near and ahead of a dry line bulge.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Line Storm is: Any thunderstorm that develops on or near a dry line.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Line is: A boundary separating moist and dry air masses, and an important factor in severe weather frequency in the Great Plains. It typically lies north-south across the central and southern high Plains states during the spring and early summer, where it separates moist air from the Gulf of Mexico (to the east) and dry desert air from the southwestern states (to the west). The dry line typically advances eastward during the afternoon and retreats westward at night. However, a strong storm system can sweep the dry line eastward into the Mississippi Valley, or even further east, regardless of the time of day. A typical dry line passage results in a sharp drop in humidity (hence the name), clearing skies, and a wind shift from south or southeasterly to west or southwesterly. (Blowing dust and rising temperatures also may follow, especially if the dry line passes during the daytime. These changes occur in reverse order when the dry line retreats westward. Severe and sometimes tornadic thunderstorms often develop along a dry line or in the moist air just to the east of it, especially when it begins moving eastward.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Microburst is: A microburst with little or no precipitation reaching the ground; most common in semi-arid regions. They may or may not produce lightning. Dry microbursts may develop in an otherwise fair-weather pattern; visible signs may include a cumulus cloud or small Cb with a high base and high-level virga, or perhaps only an orphan anvil from a dying rain shower. At the ground, the only visible sign might be a dust plume or a ring of blowing dust beneath a local area of virga.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Punch is: [Slang], a surge of drier air; normally a synoptic-scale or mesoscale process. A dry punch at the surface results in a dry line bulge. A dry punch aloft above an area of moist air at low levels often increases the potential for severe weather.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Slot is: A zone of dry (and relatively cloud-free) air which wraps east- or northeastward into the southern and eastern parts of a synoptic scale or mesoscale low pressure system. A dry slot generally is seen best on satellite photographs.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Thunderstorm is: Generally a high-based thunderstorm when lightning is observed, but little if any precipitation reaches the ground. Most of the rain produced by the thunderstorm evaporates into relatively dry air beneath the storm cell. May also be referred to as "dry lightning".

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dry Weather Flow is: In hydrologic terms, streamflow which results from precipitation that infiltrates into the soil and eventually moves through the soil to the stream channel. This is also referred to as baseflow, or ground water flow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DSA is: Special Tropical Disturbance Statement
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dst Index is: A geomagnetic index describing variations in the equatorial ringcurrent

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Duration Curve is: In hydrologic terms, a cumulative frequency curve that shows the percent of time during which specified units of items (e.g. discharge, head, power,etc.) were equaled or exceeded in a given period. It is the integral of the frequency diagram.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Duration of Ice Cover is: In hydrologic terms, The time from freeze-up to break-up of an ice cover.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Duration of Sunshine is: The amount of time sunlight was detected at a given point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dusk is: Same as Civil Dusk ; the time at which the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon in the evening. At this time objects are distinguishable but there is no longer enough light to perform any outdoor activities.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Advisory is: This product is issued when convectively-driven dust is reducing visibilities to 1 mile or less, but greater than ¼ mile. Winds of 25 mph or greater are usually required.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Devil is: A small, rapidly rotating wind that is made visible by the dust, dirt or debris it picks up. Also called a whirlwind, it develops best on clear, dry, hot afternoons
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Plume is: A non-rotating "cloud" of dust raised by straight-line winds. Often seen in a microburst or behind a gust front.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Storm Warning is: This product is issued when a convectively-driven dust storm is reducing visibilities to ¼ mile or less. Winds of 25 mph or greater are usually required.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Storm is: A severe weather condition characterized by strong winds and dust-filled air over an extensive area.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dust Whirl is: A rotating column of air rendered visible by dust.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DVV is: Downward Vertical Velocity (sinking air)

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DWNDFT is: Downdraft - A small-scale column of air that rapidly sinks toward the ground, usually accompanied by precipitation as in a shower or thunderstorm. A downburst is the result of a strong downdraft.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, DWPT is: Dew Point - A measure of atmospheric moisture. It is the temperature to which air must be cooled in order to reach saturation (assuming air pressure and moisture content are constant).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dynamic Ice is: In hydrologic terms, pressure due to a moving ice cover or drifting ice. Pressure occuring at movement of first contact termed Ice Impact Pressure
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dynamic Lifting is: The forced uplifting of air from various atmospheric processes, such as weather fronts, and cyclones.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dynamic Wave Routing Model (DWOPER) is: A computerized hydraulic routing program whose algorithms incorporate the complete one-dimensional equations of unsteady flow

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Dynamics is: Generally, any forces that produce motion or effect change. In operational meteorology, dynamics usually refer specifically to those forces that produce vertical motion in the atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E-19, Report on River Gage Station is: In hydrologic terms, a report to be completed every 5 years providing a complete history of a river station and all gages that have been used for public forecasts since the establishment of the station.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E-19a, Abridged Report on River Gage Sta is: In hydrologic terms, an abridged version of an E-19, an E-19a updates the E-19 as additional information, or changes occur at the station during the intervening five year period. An E-19a is to be completed anytime a significant change occurs at a forecast point. An E-19a is also used to take the place of an E-19 in documenting any gage history, or information of any non-forecast point (i.e; data point).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E-3, Flood Stage Report is: In hydrologic terms, a form that a Service Hydrologist/ Hydrology Focal Point completes to document the dates in which forecast points are above flood stage, as well as the crest dates and stages. Discussion of the flood event must also be included in the E-5, Monthly Report of River and Flood conditions. An E-3 report is sent to Regional Headquarters, the appropriate RFC, as well as the Office of Hydrology (OH).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E-5, Monthly Report of River and Flood c is: In hydrologic terms, a monthly narrative report covering flooding which occurred over the past month. Flood stage, flood crest and dates in which flooding occurred is covered within this report for each data point which was in flood. If the flooding involved a forecast point, an E-3 must be filled out as well. If no flooding has occurred within the past month, a climatic summary of the past month can be included as well as other interesting non-flood events, such as water supply, ice jams and the occurrence of drought. An E-5 report is sent to Regional Headquarters, the appropriate RFC, as well as the Office of Hydrology (OH).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E-7, Flood Damage Report is: In hydrologic terms, a report to be completed anytime there is reported flood damage or loss of life as a direct result of flooding. An E-7 report is sent to Regional Headquarters, as well as the Office of Hydrology (OH).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, E REGION is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a daytime layer of the earth's ionosphere roughly between the altitudes of 85 and 140 km.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Easterlies is: Any winds with components from the east.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Easterly Wave is: A low level disturbance of tropical origins. Easterly waves can develop into tropical cyclones. However, tropical cyclone development is not required in order for these systems to produce significant amounts of rainfall. The easterly waves are primarily a summer phenomenon.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ebb Current is: The movement of a tidal current away form the coast or down an estuary.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EBS is: Emergency Broadcast System
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eccentricity is: A dimensionless quantity describing the elliptical shape of a planet's orbit.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Echo Tops is: The height above ground of the center of the radar beam using the tilt, or scan, that contains the highest elevation where reflectivities greater than 18 dBZ can be detected.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Echo is: Energy back scattered from a target (precipitation, clouds, etc.) and received by and displayed on a radar screen.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ECMF is: European Center for Meteorology Forecast model.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ECMWF is: European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Operational references in forecast discussions typically refer to the ECMWF's medium-range numerical forecast model, which runs out to 10 days.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eddy is: Swirling currents of air at variance with the main current.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EDT is: Eastern Daylight Time

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effective Porosity is: In hydrologic terms, the ratio, usually expressed as a percentage, of the volume of water or other liquid which a given saturated volume of rock or soil will yield under any specified hydraulic condition, to the given volume of soil or rock.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effective Precipitation is: 1) That part of the precipitation that produces runoff. 2) A weighted average of current and antecedent precipitation that is "effective" in correlating with runoff. 3) That part of the precipitation falling on an irrigated area that is effective in meeting the consumptive use requirements.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effective Terrestrial Radiation is: The difference between upwelling infrared or terrestrial radiation emitted from the earth and the downwelling infrared radiation from the atmosphere

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effective Topography is: The topography as seen by an approaching flow, which may include not only the actual terrain but also cold air masses trapped within or adjacent to the actual topography.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effluent Seepage is: In hydrologic terms, diffuse discharge of ground water to the ground surface

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Effluent Stream is: In hydrologic terms, any watercourse in which all, or a portion of the water volume came from the Phreatic zone, or zone of saturation by way of groundwater flow, or baseflow

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, El NiÃ±o is: A warming of the ocean current along the coasts of Peru and Ecuador that is generally associated with dramatic changes in the weather patterns of the region; a major El NiÃ±o event generally occurs every 3 to 7 years and is associated with changes in the weather patterns worldwide.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Element is: One of the basic conditions of the atmosphere discussed in this FMH (wind, visibility, runway visual range, weather, obscurations, sky condition, temperature and dewpoint, and pressure). See parameter

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Elevated Convection is: Convection occurring within an elevated layer, i.e., a layer in which the lowest portion is based above the earth's surface. Elevated convection often occurs when air near the ground is relatively cool and stable, e.g., during periods of isentropic lift, when an unstable layer of air is present aloft. In cases of elevated convection, stability indices based on near-surface measurements (such as the lifted index) typically will underestimate the amount of instability present. Severe weather is possible from elevated convection, but is less likely than it is with surface-based convection.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Embankment is: In hydrologic terms, fill material, usually earth or rock, placed with sloping sides and usually with length greater than height. All dams are types of embankments
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EMC is: Environmental Modeling Center

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Emergency Action Plan is: In hydrologic terms, a predetermined plan of action to be taken to reduce the potential for property damage and loss of life in an area affected by a dam break or excessive spillway.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Emergency Services is: In hydrologic terms, services provided in order to minimize the impact of a flood that is already happening. These measures are the responsibility of city, or county emergency management staff and the owners or operators of major, or critical facilities. Some examples of emergency services are flood warning and evacuation, flood response, and post flood activities.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Emerging Flux Region (EFR) is: In solar-terrestrial terms, an area on the sun where new magnetic flux is erupting.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Emissivity is: The ability of a surface to emit radiant energy compared to that of a black body at the same temperature and with the same area.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EML is: Elevated Mixed Layer

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Energy Dissipator is: In hydrologic terms, a structure which slows fast-moving spillway flows in order to prevent erosion of the stream channel.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Energy Helicity Index is: An index that incorporates vertical shear and instability, designed for the purpose of forecasting supercell thunderstorms

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Engineer's Level is: A telescope which is attached to a spirit-tube level, all revolving around a vertical axis and is mounted on a tripod. An Engineer's Level is used for determining the difference in elevation between two points. The telescope on the level has a vertical cross hair and a horizontal cross hair. Once the instrument is leveled, the sighting through the horizontal cross hair represents a horizontal plane of equal elevation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Enhanced V is: A pattern seen on satellite infrared photographs of thunderstorms, in which a thunderstorm anvil exhibits a V-shaped region of colder cloud tops extending downwind from the thunderstorm core. The enhanced V indicates a very strong updraft, and therefore a higher potential for severe weather. Enhanced V should not be confused with V notch, which is a radar signature.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Enhanced Wording is: 1. An option used by the SPC in tornado and severe thunderstorm watches when the potential for strong/violent tornadoes, or unusually widespread damaging straight-line winds, is high. The text that accompanies a watch of this type will include the line "THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION." 2. Strong wording or emphasis used in a zone forecast issued by a National Weather Service Forecast Office highlighting a potential condition (e.g., "some thunderstorms may be severe").

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ensemble Forecast is: Multiple predictions from an ensemble of slightly different initial conditions and/or various versions of models. The objectives are to improve the accuracy of the forecast through averaging the various forecasts, which eliminates non-predictable components, and to provide reliable information on forecast uncertainties from the diversity amongst ensemble members. Forecasters use this tool to measure the likelihood of a forecast.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ensemble Hydrologic Forecasting is: In hydrologic terms, a process whereby a continuous hydrologic model is successively executed several times for the same forecast period by use of varied data input scenarios, or a perturbation of a key variable state for each model run. A common method employed to obtain a varied data input scenario is to use the historical meteorological record, with the assumption that several years of observed data covering the time period beginning on the current date and extending through the forecast period comprises a reasonable estimate of the possible range of future conditions.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ENSEMBLE is: A collection of numerical model results that show slightly different possible outcomes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ensembles is: Reference to a set of computer models run under the concept of Ensemble Forecasting : multiple predictions from an ensemble of models with slightly different initial conditions used as input and/or slightly different versions of models. The objectives are to improve the accuracy of the forecast through averaging the various forecasts, which eliminates non-predictable components, and to provide reliable information on forecast uncertainties from the diversity amongst ensemble members. Forecasters use this tool to measure the likelihood of a forecast.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion is: The CPC issues the ENSO Diagnostic Discussion around the middle of the month. The discussion addresses the current oceanic and atmospheric conditions in the Pacific and the seasonal climate outlook for the following one to three seasons.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ENSO is: Abbreviation for El NiÃ±o-Southern Oscillation , a reference to the state of the Southern Oscillation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Entrainment Zone is: A shallow region at the top of a convective boundary layer where fluid is entrained into the growing boundary layer from the overlying fluid by the collapse of rising convective plumes or bubbles.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Entrance Region is: The region upstream from a wind speed maximum in a jet stream (jet max), in which air is approaching (entering) the region of maximum winds, and therefore is accelerating. This acceleration results in a vertical circulation that creates divergence in the upper-level winds in the right half of the entrance region (as would be viewed looking along the direction of flow). This divergence results in upward motion of air in the right rear quadrant (or right entrance region) of the jet max. Severe weather potential sometimes increases in this area as a result. See also exit region, left exit region.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Entropy is: The amount of energy that is not available for work during a certain process.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Environment Canada is: The Canadian federal government department responsible for issuing weather forecasts and weather warnings in Canada.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Environmental Lapse Rate is: The rate of decrease of air temperature with height, usually measured with a radiosonde.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Environmental Temperature Sounding is: An instantaneous or near-instantaneous sounding of temperature as a function of height. This sounding or vertical profile is usually obtained by a balloon-borne instrument, but can also be measured using remote sensing equipment.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EPA is: Environmental Protection Agency
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EPV is: Equivalent Potential Vorticity

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equi-Potential Line is: In hydrologic terms, a line, in a field of flow, such that the total head is the same for all points on the line, and therefore the direction of flow is perpendicular to the line at all points.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equilibrium Drawdown is: In hydrologic terms, the ultimate, constant drawdown for a steady rate of pumped discharge.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equilibrium Level is: (EL) - On a sounding, the level above the level of free convection (LFC) at which the temperature of a rising air parcel again equals the temperature of the environment. The height of the EL is the height at which thunderstorm updrafts no longer accelerate upward. Thus, to a close approximation, it represents the height of expected (or ongoing) thunderstorm tops.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equilibrium Surface Discharge is: In hydrologic terms, the steady rate of surface discharge which results from a long-continued, steady rate of net rainfall, with discharge rate equal to net rainfall rate

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equilibrium Time is: In hydrologic terms, the time when flow conditions become substantially equal to those corresponding to equilibrium discharge or equilibrium drawdown.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equinox is: The time when the sun crosses the earth's equator, making night and day of approximately equal length all over the earth and occurring about March 21 (the spring or vernal equinox) and September 22 (autumnal equinox).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Equivalent Potential Temperature is: The equivalent potential temperature is the temperature a parcel at a specific pressure level and temperature would have if it were raised to 0 mb, condensing all moisture from the parcel, and then lowered to 1000 mb.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Erosion is: In hydrologic terms, wearing away of the lands by running water, glaciers,winds, and waves, can be subdivided into three process: Corrasion, Corrosion, and Transportation. Weathering, although sometimes included here, is a distant process which does not imply removal of any material

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eruptive Prominence on Limb (EPL) is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a solar prominence that becomes activa- ted and is seen to ascend from the sun.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eruptive is: In solar-terrestrial terms, solar activity levels with at least one radio event (10 cm) and several chromospheric events per day (Class C Flares).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ESP is: Extended Streamflow Prediction
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EST is: Eastern Standard Time

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Estuary is: In hydrologic terms, the thin zone along a coastline where freshwater systems and rivers meet and mix with a salty ocean (such as a bay, mouth of a river, salt marsh, lagoon).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Esturine waters is: In hydrologic terms, deepwater tidal habitats and tidal wetlands that are usually enclosed by land but have access to the ocean and are at least occasionally diluted by freshwater runoff from the land (such as bays, mouths of rivers, salt marshes, lagoons).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Esturine Zone is: In hydrologic terms, the area near the coastline that consists of esturaries and coastal saltwater wetlands

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eta Model is: Now referred to as North Amercian Meso (NAM) is one of the operational numerical forecast models run at NCEP. The Eta is run four times daily, with forecast output out to 84 hours.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ETA is: 1. The Eta Model, now referred to as North Amercian Meso (NAM) an 84-hour numerical model of the atmosphere run four times daily by NCEP. This is one of the main forecast models used for short-term weather prediction in the United States. 2. Estimated Time of Arrival
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporation-mixing Fog is: Fog that forms when the evaporation of water raises the dew point of the adjacent air.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporation Pan is: In hydrologic terms, a pan used to hold water during observations for the determination of the quantity of evaporation at a given location. Such pans are of varying sizes and shapes, the most commonly used being circular or square.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporation Rate is: In hydrologic terms, the quantity of water, expressed in terms of depth of liquid water, which is evaporated from a given surface per unit of time. It is usually expressed in inches depth, per day, month, or year.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporation is: The process of a liquid changing into a vapor or gas, usually water in meteorology.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI) is: An experimental drought monitoring and early warning guidance tool. It examines how anomalous the atmospheric evaporative demand is for a given location and across a time period of interest.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evaporimeter is: In hydrologic terms, an instrument which measures the evaporation rate of water into the atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Evapotranspiration is: Combination of evaporation from free water surfaces and transpiration of water from plant surfaces to the atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, EWW is: Extreme Wind Warning (EWW) inform the public of the need to take immediate shelter in an interior portion of a well-built structure due to the onset of extreme tropical cyclone winds. An EWW for extreme tropical cyclone winds should be issued when both of the following criteria are met: a. Tropical cyclone is a category 3 or greater on the Saffir Simpson hurricane scale as designated by NHC, CPHC or JTWC. b. Sustained tropical cyclone surface winds of 100 knots (115 mph) or greater are occurring or are expected to occur in a WFOâ€™s county warning area within one hour.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Excess Rain is: In hydrologic terms, effective rainfall in excess of infiltration capacity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO) is: A graphical product in which the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) forecasts the probability that rainfall will exceed flash flood guidance (FFG) within 40 kilometers (25 miles) of a point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Exclusive Flood Control Storage Capacity is: In hydrologic terms, the space in a reservoir reserved for the sole purpose of regulating flood inflows to abate flood damage

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Exit Region is: The region downstream from a wind speed maximum in a jet stream (jet max), in which air is moving away from the region of maximum winds, and therefore is decelerating. This deceleration results in divergence in the upper-level winds in the left half of the exit region (as would be viewed looking along the direction of flow). This divergence results in upward motion of air in the left front quadrant (or left exit region) of the jet max. Severe weather potential sometimes increases in this area as a result. See also entrance region, right entrance region.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Exosphere is: The upper most layer of the earth's atmosphere; the only layer where atmospheric gases can escape into outer space.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Experimental Product is: An experimental product is in the final stages of testing and evaluation. If the product proves accurate and valuable to users then the next step is to make it an operational product.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Explosive Deepening is: A decrease in the minimum sea-level pressure of a tropical cyclone of 2.5 mb/hr for at least 12 hours or 5 mb/hr for at least six hours.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extended Forecast Discussion is: This discussion is issued once a day around 2 PM EST (3 PM EDT) and is primarily intended to provide insight into guidance forecasts for the 3- to 5-day forecast period. The geographic focus of this discussion is on the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii). Although portions of this narrative will parallel the Hemispheric Map Discussion, a much greater effort is made to routinely relate the model forecasts and necessary modifications to weather forecasts, mainly in terms of temperature and precipitation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extraterrestrial Radiation is: The theoretically-calculated radiation flux from the sun at the top of the atmosphere, before losses by atmospheric absorption.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extratropical Cyclone is: A cyclone in the middle and high latitudes often being 2000 kilometers in diameter and usually containing a cold front that extends toward the equator for hundreds of kilometers.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extratropical Low is: A low pressure center which refers to a migratory frontal cyclone of middle and higher latitudes. Tropical cyclones occasionally evolve into extratropical lows losing tropical characteristics and become associated with frontal discontinuity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extratropical is: A term used in advisories and tropical summaries to indicate that a cyclone has lost its "tropical" characteristics. The term implies both poleward displacement of the cyclone and the conversion of the cyclone's primary energy source from the release of latent heat of condensation to baroclinic (the temperature contrast between warm and cold air masses) processes. It is important to note that cyclones can become extratropical and still retain winds of hurricane or tropical storm force.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Cold Warning is: This product is issued when dangerously cold air temperatures or wind chill values are expected or occurring. The criteria for this warning varies from place to place.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Cold Watch is: This product is issued when an extreme cold event is possible, but its occurrence, location, and/or timing is still uncertain.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Cold is: Extreme Cold: A period of abnormally cold and dangerous temperatures or wind chills that can result in negative impacts to people, animals, and infrastructure

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Heat Warning is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when extremely dangerous heat is expected or occurring. The criteria for this warning varies from place to place.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Heat Watch is: This product is issued when conditions are favorable for an extreme heat event but its occurrence, location, and/or timing is still uncertain.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Heat is: A period of abnormally hot and dangerous temperatures, with or without high humidities, that can result in negative impacts to people, animals, and infrastructure.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) is: A portion of the electromagnetic spectrum from approximately 100 to 1000 angstroms.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extreme Wind Warning is: Extreme Wind Warning (EWW) inform the public of the need to take immediate shelter in an interior portion of a well-built structure due to the onset of extreme tropical cyclone winds. An EWW for extreme tropical cyclone winds should be issued when both of the following criteria are met: a. Tropical cyclone is a category 3 or greater on the Saffir Simpson hurricane scale as designated by NHC, CPHC or JTWC. b. Sustained tropical cyclone surface winds of 100 knots (115 mph) or greater are occurring or are expected to occur in a WFOâ€™s county warning area within one hour.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Extremely Low Frequency (ELF) is: That portion of the radio frequency spectrum from 30 to 3000 hertz

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eye Wall is: It is an organized band of cumuliform clouds that immediately surrounds the center (eye) of a hurricane. The fiercest winds and most intense rainfall typically occur near the eye wall. VIP levels 3 or greater are typical. Eye wall and wall cloud are used synonymously, but it should not be confused with a wall cloud of thunderstorm.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Eye is: The relatively calm center in a hurricane that is more than one half surrounded by wall cloud. The winds are light, the skies are partly cloudy or even clear (the skies are usually free of rain) and radar depicts it as an echo-free area within the eye wall.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, F Corona is: In solar-terrestrial terms, of the white-light corona (that is, the corona seen by the eye at a total solar eclipse), that portion which is caused by sunlight scattered or reflected by solid particles (dust) in inter-planetary space.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, F Region is: In solar-terrestrial terms, the upper layer of the ionosphere, approximately 120 to 1500 km in altitude. The F region is subdivided into the F1 and F2 regions. The F2 region is the most dense and peaks at altitudes between 200 and 600 km. The F1 region is a smaller peak in electron density, which forms at lower altitudes in the daytime.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, F Scale is: Abbreviation for Fujita Scale , a system of rating the intensity of tornadoes; for detailed information, see the definition for that term.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, F is: 1) Fahrenheit- The standard scale used to measure temperature in the United States. On this scale, the freezing point of water is 32Â°F and the boiling point is 212Â°F. To convert a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit, multiply it by 9/5 and then add 32: Â°F = (Â°C * 9/5) + 32 or 2) Fog- Water droplets suspended in the air at the Earth's surface. Fog is often hazardous when the visibility is reduced to Â¼ mile or less.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FAA is: Federal Aviation Administration
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Face is: In hydrologic terms, the external surface of a structure, such as the surface of a dam.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Facula is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a bright region of the photosphere seen in white light, seldom visible except near the solar limb.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fahrenheit is: (abbrev. F) The standard scale used to measure temperature in the United States. On this scale, the freezing point of water is 32Â°F and the boiling point is 212Â°F. To convert a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit, multiply it by 9/5 and then add 32: Â°F = (Â°C * 9/5) + 32

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fair is: It is usually used at night to describe less than 3/8 opaque clouds, no precipitation, no extremes of visibility, temperature or winds. It describes generally pleasant weather conditions.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fall Line is: A skiing term, indicating the line of steepest descent of a slope.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fall Wind is: A strong, cold, downslope wind.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fall is: the season of the year which is the transition period from summer to winter occurring as the sun approaches the winter solstice. In the Northern Hemisphere, fall customarily includes the months of September, October and November.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fallstreak is: Same as Virga ; streaks or wisps of precipitation falling from a cloud but evaporating before reaching the ground. In certain cases, shafts of virga may precede a microburst.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FAN is: AVN MOS Guidance (older version)

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fanning is: A pattern of plume dispersion in a stable atmosphere, in which the plume fans out in the horizontal and meanders about at a fixed height.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fathom is: Unit of water depth equal to 6 feet.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FAWS is: Flight Advisory Weather Service

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FBO is: (Great Lakes Freeze-Up/Break-Up Outlook) - A National Weather Service product to keep mariners informed of the projected freeze-up date or break-up date of ice on the Great Lakes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Federal Snow Sampler is: In hydrologic terms, a snow sampler consisting of five or more sections of sampling tubes, one which has a steel cutter on the end. The combined snowpack measuring depth is 150 inches. This instrument was formerly the Mount Rose Type Snow Sampling Set.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Feeder Bands is: Lines or bands of low-level clouds that move (feed) into the updraft region of a thunderstorm, usually from the east through south (i.e., parallel to the inflow). Same as inflow bands. This term also is used in tropical meteorology to describe spiral-shaped bands of convection surrounding, and moving toward, the center of a tropical cyclone.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FEMA is: Federal Emergency Management Agency. An agency of the federal government having responsibilities in hazard mitigation; FEMA also administers the National Flood Insurance Program.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ferrel Cell is: In the general circulation of the atmosphere, the name given to the middle latitude cell marked by sinking motion near 30 degrees and rising motion near 60 degrees latitude.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fetch is: 1. The area in which ocean waves are generated by the wind. Also refers to the length of the fetch area, measured in the direction of the wind. 2. In hydrologic terms, The effective distance which waves have traversed in open water, from their point of origin to the point where they break. 2. The distance of the water or the homogenous type surface over which the wind blows without appreciable change in direction.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Few Clouds is: An official sky cover classification for aviation weather observations, descriptive of a sky cover of 1/8 to 2/8. This is applied only when obscuring phenomenon aloft are present--that is, not when obscuring phenomenon are surface-based, such as fog.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Few is: A National Weather Service convective precipitation descriptor for a 10 percent chance of measurable precipitation (0.01 inch). Few is used interchangeably with isolated.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FFG is: Flash Flood Guidance

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, FG is: (Also abbrev. F) - Fog - water droplets suspended in the air at the Earth's surface. Fog is often hazardous when the visibility is reduced to Â¼ mile or less.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fibril is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a linear pattern in the H-alpha chromosphere of the sun, as seen through an H-alpha filter, occurring near strong sunspots and plage or in filament channels.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Field (Moisture) Capacity is: The amount of water held in soil against the pull of gravity
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Field Moisture Deficiency is: The quantity of water, which would be required to restore the soil moisture to field moisture capacity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Filament Channel is: A broad pattern of fibrils in the chromosphere, marking where a filament may soon form or where a filament recently disappeared.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Filament is: A mass of gas suspended over the photosphere by magnetic fields and seen as dark lines threaded over the solar disk. A filament on the limb of the sun seen in emission against the dark sky is called a prominence.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fill Dam is: In hydrologic terms, any dam constructed of excavated natural materials or of industrial wastes
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Filling is: The opposite of deepening. A general increase in the central pressure of a low pressure system.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Fire Wind is: A thermally driven wind blowing radially inward toward a fire, produced by horizontal temperature differences between the heated air above the fire and the surrounding cooler free atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Firebrand is: Any source of heat, natural or man made, capable of igniting wildland fuels; flaming or glowing fuel particles that can be carried naturally by wind, convection currents, or gravity into unburned fuels.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Firn Line is: In hydrologic terms, the highest level to which the fresh snow on a glacier's surface retreats during the melting season. The line separating the accumulation area from the ablation area

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Firn (Snow) is: In hydrologic terms, old snow on top of glaciers, granular and compact and not yet converted into ice. It is a transitional stage between snow and ice. Also called Neve.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, First Law of Thermodynamics is: The law of physics that states that the heat absorbed by a system either raises the internal energy of the system or does work on the environment.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Flanking Line is: A line of cumulus or towering cumulus clouds connected to and extending outward from the most active part of a supercell, normally on the southwest side. The line normally has a stair-step appearance, with the tallest clouds closest to the main storm

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Flare is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a sudden eruption of energy on the solar disk lasting minutes to hours, from which radiation and particles are emitted

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Flash Flood Guidance is: (FFG) Forecast guidance produced by the River Forecast Centers, often model output, specific to the potential for flash flooding (e.g., how much rainfall over a given area will be required to produce flash flooding).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Flash Flood Statement is: (FFS) In hydrologic terms, a statement by the NWS which provides follow-up information on flash flood watches and warnings.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Flash Flood Table is: In hydrologic terms, a table of pre-computed forecast crest stage values for small streams for a variety of antecedent moisture conditions and rain amounts. Soil moisture conditions are often represented by flash flood guidance values. In lieu of crest stages, categorical representations of flooding, e.g., minor, moderate, etc. may be used on the tables.
