In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, High Water Probability is: The probability (%) that a stream will reach its high water flow within the forecast period.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, High Wind Warning is: This product is issued when sustained, strong winds with even stronger gusts are expected or occurring. Generally for sustained wind speeds of 40 mph or greater lasting for 1 hour or longer, or winds of 58 mph or greater for any duration.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, High Wind Watch is: This product is issued when a high wind event is possible, but its occurrence, location, and/or timing is still uncertain.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, High Wind is: Sustained wind speeds of 40 mph or greater lasting for 1 hour or longer, or winds of 58 mph or greater for any duration.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, High is: (abbrev. HI)- In meteorology, a region of high pressure; also known as anticyclone.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hinge Crack is: In hydrologic terms, a crack caused by significant changes in water level.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HLS is: Hurricane Local Statement

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HMD is: (Hemispheric Map Discussion)- This discussion is issued once a day around 1 PM EST (2 PM EDT) and is primarily intended to provide insight into the hemispheric circulation patterns over the next 5 days. This includes a discussion of the 5-day mean circulation pattern. Comparisons, differences, and continuity among the numerical models are highlighted, and preferred solutions are proposed with an explanation of why a solution is preferred. This includes any reasons why the preferred solution differs from any model. In cases where certain models are not universally available, an attempt will be made to describe that model's solution to an extent that a reader can understand it's important aspects.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hoar Frost is: A deposit of interlocking crystals formed by direct sublimation on objects, usually those of small diameter freely exposed to the air, such as tree branches, plants, wires, poles, etc. The deposition of hoar frost is similar to the process by which dew is formed, except that the temperature of the frosted object must be below freezing. It forms when air with a dew point below freezing is brought to saturation by cooling.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hodograph is: A polar coordinate graph which shows the vertical wind profile of the lowest 7000 meters of the atmosphere. These plots are used to determine the advection patterns aloft, whether a thunderstorm will rotate, and the type of thunderstorms that you will likely see that day.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Homologous Flares is: In solar-terrestrial terms, solar flares that occur repetitively in the same active region, with essentially the same position and with a common pattern of development

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hook Echo is: A radar reflectivity pattern characterized by a hook-shaped extension of a thunderstorm echo, usually in the right-rear part of the storm (relative to its direction of motion). A hook often is associated with a mesocyclone, and indicates favorable conditions for tornado development.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Horizon is: The distant line along which the earth and sky appear to meet. Obstructions are not considered as part of the horizon.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hourly Precipitation Data (HPD) is: It contains data on nearly 3,000 hourly precipitation stations (National Weather Service, Federal Aviation Administration, and cooperative observer stations) in inches to tenths or inches to hundredths at local standard time. HPD includes maximum precipitation for nine (9) time periods from 15 minutes to 24 hours, for selected stations.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HP Storm is: or HP Supercell - High-Precipitation storm (or High-Precipitation supercell). A supercell thunderstorm in which heavy precipitation (often including hail) falls on the trailing side of the mesocyclone. Precipitation often totally envelops the region of rotation, making visual identification of any embedded tornadoes difficult and very dangerous. Unlike most classic supercells, the region of rotation in many HP storms develops in the front-flank region of the storm (i.e., usually in the eastern portion). HP storms often produce extreme and prolonged downburst events, serious flash flooding, and very large damaging hail events.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, hPa is: Hectopascal- A unit of pressure equal to a millibar (1 hPa = 1 mb).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HPC is: Hydrometeorological Prediction Center

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HSA (Hydrologic Service Area) is: A geographical area assigned to Weather Service Forecast Office's/Weather Forecast Office's that embraces one or more rivers.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Humidity Recovery is: The change in relative humidity over a given period of time; generally between late evening and sunrise. The moisture change in the fine fuels during this period is directly related to the amount of humidity recovery.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Humidity is: Generally, a measure of the water vapor content of the air. Popularly, it is used synonymously with relative humidity.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hummock is: In hydrologic terms, a hillock of broken ice which has been forced upward by pressure
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hummocked Ice is: In hydrologic terms, ice piled haphazardly one piece over another to form an uneven surface.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Force Wind Warning is: A warning for sustained winds, or frequent gusts, of 64 knots (74 mph) or greater, either predicted or occurring, and not directly associated with a tropical cyclone.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Force Wind Watch is: A watch for an increased risk of a hurricane force wind event for sustained surface winds, or frequent gusts, of 34 knots 64 knots (74 mph) or greater, but its occurrence, location, and/or timing is still uncertain.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Local Statement is: A public release prepared by local National Weather Service offices in or near a threatened area giving specific details for its county/parish warning area on (1) weather conditions (2) evacuation decisions made by local officials (3) other precautions necessary to protect life and property.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Season is: The part of the year having a relatively high incidence of tropical cyclones. In the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf of Mexico, and central North Pacific, the hurricane season is the period from June through November; in the eastern Pacific, May 15 through November 30. Tropical cyclones can occur year-round in any basin.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Warning is: An announcement that hurricane conditions (sustained winds of 74 mph or higher) are expected somewhere within the specified coastal area. Because hurricane preparedness activities become difficult once winds reach tropical storm force, the hurricane warning is issued 36 hours in advance of the anticipated onset of tropical-storm-force winds. The warning can remain in effect when dangerously high water or a combination of dangerously high water and waves continue, even though winds may be less than hurricane force.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane Watch is: An announcement that hurricane conditions (sustained winds of 74 mph or higher) are possible within the specified coastal area. Because hurricane preparedness activities become difficult once winds reach tropical storm force, the hurricane watch is issued 48 hours in advance of the anticipated onset of tropical-storm-force winds.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hurricane is: (abbrev. HURCN) A tropical cyclone in the Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, or eastern Pacific, which the maximum 1-minute sustained surface wind is 64 knots (74 mph) or greater.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HWRF is: NWS/Hurricane Weather Research and Forecasting Model

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hyder Flare is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a filiment-associated two-ribbon flare, often occurring in spotless regions. The flare presumably results from the impact on the chromosphere of infalling filament material.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Fill Dam is: In hydrologic terms, a dam constructed of materials, often dredged, that are conveyed and placed by suspension in flowing water
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Flow is: Atmospheric flow that is similar in character to the flow of water over an obstacle.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Grade Line is: In hydrologic terms, a line whose plotted ordinate position represents the sum of pressure head plus elevation head for the various positions along a given fluid flow path, such as along a pipeline or a ground water streamline.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Head is: In hydrologic terms, (1) The height of the free surface of a body of water above a given point beneath the surface. (2) The height of the water level at the headworks, or an upstream point, of a waterway, and the water surface at a given point downstream. (3) The height of a hydraulic grade line above the center line of a pressure pipe, at a given point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Jump is: A steady disturbance in the lee of a mountain, where the airflow passing over the mountain suddenly changes from a region of low depth and high velocity to a region of high depth and low velocity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydraulic Permeability is: In hydrologic terms, the flow of water through a unit cross-sectional area of soil normal to the direction of flow when the hydraulic gradient is unity.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HydroÂ­meteorology is: An interÂ­disciÂ­plinary science involving the study and analysis of the interÂ­relationÂ­ships between the atmoÂ­spheric and land phases of water as it moves through the hydroÂ­logic cycle.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrograph Separation is: In hydrologic terms, the process where the storm hydrograph is separated into baseflow components and surface runoff components.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrograph is: In hydrologic terms, a graph showing the water level (stage), discharge, or other property of a river volume with respect to time.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrographic Survey is: In hydrologic terms, an instrumental survey to measure and determine characteristics of streams and other bodies of water within an area, including such things as location, areal extent, and depth of water in lakes or the ocean; the width, depth, and course of streams; position and elevation of high water marks; location and depth of wells, etc.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Budget is: In hydrologic terms, an accounting of the inflow to, outflow from, and storage in, a hydrologic unit, such as a drainage basin, aquifer, soil zone, lake, reservoir, or irrigation project.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Cycle is: The description of the transport of water substance between the earth, the atmosphere, and the seas. or In hydrologic terms, the natural pathway water follows as it changes between liquid, solid, and gaseous states.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Ensemble Forecast System (HEFS) is: A probabilistic forecast tool with the goals to provide hydrologic forecasts including an analysis of â€œprobable outcomesâ€ and to minimize biases in the atmospheric models and in the hydrologic models.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Equation is: In hydrologic terms, the water inventory equation (Inflow = Outflow + Change in Storage) which expresses the basic principle that during a given time interval the total inflow to an area must equal the total outflow plus the net change in storage.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Model is: In hydrologic terms, a conceptual or physically-based procedure for numerically simulating a process or processes which occur in a watershed.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrologic Service Area is: HSA. A geographical area assigned to Weather Service Forecast Office's/Weather Forecast Office's that embraces one or more rivers.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrology is: The scientific study of the waters of the earth, especially with relation to the effects of precipitation and evaporation upon the occurrence and character of water on or below the land surface.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrometeor is: A particle of condensed water (liquid, snow, ice, graupel, hail) in the atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrometeorologists is: In hydrologic terms, individuals who have the combined knowledge in the fields of both meteorology and hydrology which enables them to study and solve hydrologic problems where meteorology is a factor.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrometeorology is: An interÂ­disciÂ­plinary science involving the study and analysis of the interÂ­relationÂ­ships between the atmoÂ­spheric and land phases of water as it moves through the hydroÂ­logic cycle.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrostatic Head is: In hydrologic terms, a measure of pressure at a given point in a liquid in terms of the vertical height of a column of the same liquid which would produce the same pressure
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hyetograph is: A graphical representation of rainfall intensity with respect to time.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hygrometer is: An instrument which measures the humidity of the air.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hygroscopic is: Absorbing or attracting moisture from the air.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Hypothermia is: A rapid, progressive mental and physical collapse that accompanies the lowering of body temperature.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, HZ is: 1) Haze- An aggregation in the atmosphere of very fine, widely dispersed, solid or liquid particles, or both, giving the air an opalescent appearance that subdues colors. (or) 2) Hertz- An international unit of frequency equal to one cycle per second, and named after a German physicist.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Age is: A time of widespread glaciation.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Boom is: In hydrologic terms, a floating structure designed to retain ice.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Bridge is: In hydrologic terms, a continuous ice cover of limited size extending from shore to shore like a bridge.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Crystals is: A barely visible crystalline form of ice that has the shape of needles, columns or plates. Ice crystals are so small that they seem to be suspended in air. Ice crystals occur at very low temperatures in a stable atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Fog is: (Also called ice-crystal fog, frozen fog, frost fog, frost flakes, air hoar, rime fog, pogonip.) A type of fog, composed of suspended particles of ice; partly ice crystals 20 to 100 micron in diameter, but chiefly (especially when dense) ice particles about 12â€“20 micron in diameter, formed by direct freezing of supercooled water droplets with little growth directly from the vapor. It occurs at very low temperatures, and usually in clear, calm weather in high latitudes. The sun is usually visible and may cause halo phenomena. Ice fog is rare at temperatures warmer than -30Â°C, and increases in frequency with decreasing temperature until it is almost always present at air temperatures of -45Â°C in the vicinity of a source of water vapor. Such sources are the open water of fast-flowing streams or of the sea, herds of animals, volcanoes, and especially products of combustion for heating or propulsion. At temperatures warmer than -30Â°C, these sources can cause steam fog of liquid water droplets, which may turn into ice fog when cooled (see frost smoke). See ice-crystal haze, arctic mist.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Gorge is: In hydrologic terms, the gorge or opening left in a jam after it has broken.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Jam is: In hydrologic terms, a stationary accumulation that restricts or blocks streamflow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Nucleus is: Any particle that serves as a nucleus in the formation of ice crystals in the atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Pellets is: (abbrev. IP) Same as Sleet ; defined as pellets of ice composed of frozen or mostly frozen raindrops or refrozen partially melted snowflakes. These pellets of ice usually bounce after hitting the ground or other hard surfaces. A Winter Storm Warning is issued for sleet or a combination of sleet and snow based on total accumulation which is locally defined by area.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Push is: In hydrologic terms, compression of an ice cover particularly at the front of a moving section of ice cover.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Run is: In hydrologic terms, flow of ice in a river. An ice run may be light or heavy, and may consist of frazil, anchor, slush, or sheet ice
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Shove is: In hydrologic terms, on-shore ice push caused by wind, and currents, changes in temperature, etcetera.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Storm Warning is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when freezing rain produces a significant and possibly damaging accumulation of ice. The criteria for this warning varies from state to state, but typically will be issued any time more than 1/4" of ice is expected to accumulate in an area.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Storm is: An ice storm is used to describe occasions when damaging accumulations of ice are expected during freezing rain situations. Significant accumulations of ice pull down trees and utility lines resulting in loss of power and communication. These accumulations of ice make walking and driving extremely dangerous. Significant ice accumulations are usually accumulations of Â¼" or greater.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ice Twitch is: In hydrologic terms, downstream movement of a small section of an ice cover. Ice twitches occur suddenly and often appear successively.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Iceberg is: A piece of a glacier which has broken off and is floating in the sea.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Icelandic Low is: A semi-permanent, subpolar area of low pressure in the North Atlantic Ocean. Because of its broad area and range of central pressure, it is an area where migratory lows tend to slow down and deepen. It is strongest during a Northern Hemisphere winter and early spring, centered over Iceland and southern Greenland, and is the dominate weather feature in the area. During the summer, it is weaker, less intense, and might divide into two parts, one west of Iceland, the other over the Davis Strait between Greenland and Baffin Island. Then the Azores or Bermuda High becomes the dominate weather feature in the North Atlantic.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Icing is: A coating of ice on a solid object.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ideal Gas Laws is: The thermodynamic laws applying to perfect gases.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, IFR is: Instrument Flight Rules
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Impermeable is: Material that does not permit fluids to pass through it.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Impervious is: In hydrologic terms, the ability to repel water, or not let water infiltrate

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, IMPL is: Impulse- Alternate term for Upper Level System and Shortwave; a general term for any large-scale or mesoscale disturbance capable of producing upward motion (lift) in the middle or upper parts of the atmosphere.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Import is: In hydrologic terms, water piped or channeled into an area

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Impulse is: (abbrev. IMPL) Alternate term for Upper Level System and Shortwave ; a general term for any large-scale or mesoscale disturbance capable of producing upward motion (lift) in the middle or upper parts of the atmosphere.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, In-Cloud Lightning is: (abbrev. IC) Lightning that takes place within the cloud.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inactive Storage Capacity is: In hydrologic terms, the portion of capacity below which the reservoir is not normally drawn, and which is provided for sedimentation, recreation, fish and wildlife, aesthetic reasons, or for the creation of a minimum controlled operational or power head in compliance with operating agreements or restrictions.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inch-Degrees is: The product of rainfall (in inches) multiplied by the temperature (in degrees Fahrenheit) above freezing. Used as a measure of the snowmelting capacity of rainfall.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inches of Mercury is: (or in Hg) Unit of atmospheric pressure used in the United States. The name comes from the use of mercurial barometers which equate the height of a column of mercury with air pressure. One inch of mercury is equivalent to 33.86 millibars or 25.40 millimeters. See barometric pressure. First divised in 1644 by Evangelista Torricelli (1608-1647), an Italian physicist and mathematician, to explain the fundamental principles of hydromechanics. To convert millibars (mb) to inches of mercury (in Hg), divide the millibar reading by 33.86: in Hg = mb / 33.86
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inches of Runoff is: In hydrologic terms, the volume of water from runoff of a given depth over the entire drainage
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Index of Wetness is: The ratio of precipitation for a given year over the mean annual precipitation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Indirect Hit is: Generally refers to locations that do not experience a direct hit from a tropical cyclone, but do experience hurricane force winds (either sustained or gusts) or tides of at least 4 feet above normal.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Industrial Consumption is: The quantity of water consumed in a municipality or district for mechanical, trade, and manufacturing purposes, in a given period, generally one day. The per capita use is generally based on the total population of the locality, municipality, or district.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Infiltration Capacity is: In hydrologic terms, the maximum rate at which water can enter the soil at a particular point under a given set of conditions.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Infiltration Index is: In hydrologic terms, an average rate of infiltration, in inches per hour, equal to the average rate of rainfall such as that the volume of rainfall at greater rates equals the total direct runoff.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Infiltration Rate is: In hydrologic terms, (1) The rate at which infiltration takes place expressed in depth of water per unit time, usually in inches per hour. (2) The rate, usually expressed in cubic feet per second, or million gallons per day per mile of waterway, at which ground water enters an infiltration ditch or gallery, drain, sewer, or other underground conduit.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Infiltration is: In hydrologic terms, movement of water through the soil surface into the soil

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inflow Bands is: Bands of low clouds, arranged parallel to the low-level winds and moving into or toward a thunderstorm. They may indicate the strength of the inflow of moist air into the storm, and, hence, its potential severity. Spotters should be especially wary of inflow bands that are curved in a manner suggesting cyclonic rotation; this pattern may indicate the presence of a mesocyclone
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inflow Jets is: Local jets of air near the ground flowing inward toward the base of a tornado.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inflow Notch is: A radar signature characterized by an indentation in the reflectivity pattern on the inflow side of the storm. The indentation often is V-shaped, but this term should not be confused with V-notch. Supercell thunderstorms often exhibit inflow notches, usually in the right quadrant of a classic supercell, but sometimes in the eastern part of an HP storm or in the rear part of a storm (rear inflow notch).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inflow Stinger is: A beaver tail cloud with a stinger-like shape.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Influent Seepage is: In hydrologic terms, movement of gravity water in the zone of aeration from the ground surface toward the water table.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Influent Stream is: In hydrologic terms, any watercourse in which all, or a portion of the surface water flows back into the ground namely the, vadose zone, or zone of aeration

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Infrared Satellite Imagery is: This satellite imagery senses surface and cloud top temperatures by measuring the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation emitted from these objects. This energy is called "infrared". High clouds are very cold, so they appear white. Mid-level clouds are somewhat warmer, so they will be a light gray shade. Low cloud are warmer still, so they appear as a dark shade of gray or black. Often, low clouds are the same temperature as the surrounding terrain and cannot be distinguished at all. The satellite picks up this infrared energy between 10.5 and 12.6 micrometer (um) channels.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Initial Detention is: In hydrologic terms, the volume of water on the ground, either in depressions or in transit, at the time active runoff begins.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inland freshwater wetlands is: In hydrologic terms, swamps, marshes, and bogs found inland beyond the coastal saltwater wetlands.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Insolation is: Incoming solar radiation. Solar heating; sunshine.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Instability is: (abbrev. INSTBY)- The tendency for air parcels to accelerate when they are displaced from their original position; especially, the tendency to accelerate upward after being lifted. Instability is a prerequisite for severe weather - the greater the instability, the greater the potential for severe thunderstorms.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, INSTBY is: Instability- The tendency for air parcels to accelerate when they are displaced from their original position; especially, the tendency to accelerate upward after being lifted. Instability is a prerequisite for severe weather - the greater the instability, the greater the potential for severe thunderstorms.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Instrument Flight Rules is: Refers to the general weather conditions pilots can expect at the surface and applies to the weather situations at an airport during which a pilot must use instruments to assist take off and landing. IFR conditions for fixed wing aircraft means the minimum cloud ceiling is greater than 500 feet and less than 1,000 feet and/or visibility is greater than 1 mile and less than 3 miles.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Instrument Shelter is: A boxlike structure designed to protect temperature measuring instruments from exposure to direct sunshine, precipitation, and condensation, while at the same time time providing adequate ventilation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Intangible Flood Damage is: In hydrologic terms, estimates of the damage done by disruption of business, danger to health, shock, and loss of life and in general all costs not directly measurable which require a large element of judgment for estimating.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interbasin Transfer is: In hydrologic terms, the physical transfer of water from one watershed to another.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interception Storage Requirements is: In hydrologic terms, water caught by plants at the onset of a rainstorm. This must be met before rainfall reaches the ground.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interception is: In hydrologic terms, the process by which precipitation is caught and held by foliage, twigs, and branches of trees, shrubs, and other vegetation, and lost by evaporation, never reaching the surface of the ground. Interception equals the precipitation on the vegetation minus streamflow and through fall.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interflow is: In hydrologic terms, the lateral motion of water through the upper layers until it enters a stream channel. This usually takes longer to reach stream channels than runoff. This also called subsurface storm flow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Intermediate Synoptic Times is: The times of 0300, 0900, 1500, and 2100 UTC.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Intermittent Stream is: In hydrological terms, a stream that flows periodically

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, International Date Line is: The line of longitude located at 180 degrees East or West (with a few local deviations) where the date changes by a day. West of the line it is one day later than east of the line.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interplanetary Magnetic Field is: (abbrev. IMF) In solar-terrestrial terms, the magnetic field carried with the solar wind.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Interpolate is: To estimate a value within an interval between two known values. This technique is sometimes used with computer models for locations in between the model's "gridpoints."

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Intertropical Convergence Zone is: (ITCZ) The region where the northeasterly and southeasterly trade winds converge, forming an often continuous band of clouds or thunderstorms near the equator.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Intraseasonal Oscillation is: Oscillation with variability on a timescale less than a season. One example is the Madden-Julian Oscillation.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inundation is: The process of covering normally dry areas with flood waters.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Inversion is: (abbrev. INVRN) Generally, a departure from the usual increase or decrease in an atmospheric property with altitude. Specifically it almost always refers to a temperature inversion, i.e., an increase in temperature with height, or to the layer within which such an increase occurs. An inversion is present in the lower part of a cap.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, INVRN is: Inversion- Generally, a departure from the usual increase or decrease in an atmospheric property with altitude. Specifically it almost always refers to a temperature inversion, i.e., an increase in temperature with height, or to the layer within which such an increase occurs. An inversion is present in the lower part of a cap.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ionosphere is: A complex atmospheric zone of ionized gases that extends between 50 and 400 miles (80 to 640 kilometers) above the earth's surface. It is located between the mesosphere and the exosphere and is included as part of the thermosphere.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ionospheric Storm is: A disturbance in the F region of the ionosphere, which occurs in connection with geomagnetic activity
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, IP is: Ice pellets (sleet). See "PL"
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, IR is: Infrared Satellite Imagery

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Iridescence is: Brilliant spots or borders of colors in clouds, usually red and green, caused by diffraction of light by small cloud particles. The phenomenon is usually observed in thin cirrus clouds within about 30Â° of the sun and is characterized by bands of color in the cloud that contour the cloud edges.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Iridescent Clouds is: Clouds that exhibit brilliant bright spots, bands, or borders of colors, usually red and green, observed up to about 30 degrees from the sun. The coloration is due to the diffraction with small cloud particles producing the effect. It is usually seen in thin cirrostratus, cirrocumulus, and altocumulus clouds.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Irrigation Requirement is: In hydrologic terms, the quantity of water, exclusive of precipitation, that is required for crop production. It includes surface evaporation and other economically unavoidable wastes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Irrigation is: In hydrologic terms, the controlled application of water to arable lands to supply water requirements not satisfied by rainfall
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isallobar is: A line of equal change in atmospheric pressure during a specified time period.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isentropic Analysis is: A way in the forecaster can look at the atmosphere in 3-dimensions instead of looking at constant pressure surfaces (such as the 850 mb, 700 mb, 500 mb, etc.) which are in 2-dimensions. In this analysis method, the forecaster looks at constant potential temperature (the temperature that it would take if we compressed or expanded it adiabatically to the pressure of 1000 mb) surfaces. Air parcels move up and down these surfaces; therefore, the forecaster can see where the moisture is located and how much moisture is available.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isentropic Lift is: Lifting of air that is traveling along an upward-sloping isentropic surface. Isentropic lift often is referred to erroneously as overrunning, but more accurately describes the physical process by which the lifting occurs. Situations involving isentropic lift often are characterized by widespread stratiform clouds and precipitation, but may include elevated convection in the form of embedded thunderstorms.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isentropic Surface is: A two-dimensional surface containing points of equal potential temperature.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isobar is: A line connecting points of equal pressure.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isobaric Chart is: A weather map representing conditions on a surface of equal atmospheric pressure. For example, a 500 mb chart will display conditions at the level of the atmosphere at which the atmospheric pressure is 500 mb. The height above sea level at which the pressure is that particular value may vary from one location to another at any given time, and also varies with time at any one location, so it does not represent a surface of constant altitude/height (i.e., the 500 mb level may be at a different height above sea level over Dallas than over New York).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isobaric Process is: Any thermodynamic change of state of a system that takes a place at constant pressure.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isobath is: In hydrologic terms, an imaginary line on the earth's surface or a line on a map connecting all points which are the same vertical distance above the upper or lower surface of a water-bearing formation or aquifer

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isochrone is: A line on a chart connecting equal times of occurrence of an event. In a weather analysis, a sequence plotted on a map of the frontal positions at several different observation times would constitute a set of isochrones.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isodop is: A contour of constant Doppler velocity values.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isodrosotherm is: A line connecting points of equal dew point temperature.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isoheight is: Same as a contour depicting vertical height of some surface above a datum plane.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isohel is: A line on a weather map connecting points receiving equal sunlight.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isohyet is: A line connected points of equal precipitation amounts.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isolated is: A National Weather Service convective precipitation descriptor for a 10 percent chance of measurable precipitation (0.01 inch). Isolated is used interchangeably with few.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isopleth is: A broad term for any line on a weather map connecting points with equal values of a particular atmospheric variable (temperature, dew point, etc.). Isotherms, isotachs, etc. are all examples of isopleths.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isotach is: A line connecting points of equal wind speed.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isotherm is: A line connecting points of equal temperature.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Isotropic is: Having the same characteristics in all directions, as with isotropic antennas. Directional or focused antennas are not isotropic.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Issuance Time is: The time the product is transmitted.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ITCZ is: Inter-tropical Convergence Zone. The region where the northeasterly and southeasterly tradewinds converge, forming an often continuous band of clouds or thunderstorms near the equator
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ITWAS is: Integrated Terminal Weather System
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, J/kg is: Joules per kilogram, unit commonly used to represent CAPE and CIN.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, January Thaw is: A period of mild weather popularly supposed to recur each year in late January.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet Max is: ( or Jet Streak) A point or area of relative maximum wind speeds within a jet stream.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet Streak is: Same as Jet Max ; a point or area ("streak") of relative maximum wind speeds within a jet stream.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet Stream Cirrus is: A loose term for filamentous cirrus that appears to radiate from a point in the sky, and exhibits characteristics associated with strong vertical wind shear, such as twisted or curved filaments.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet Stream is: (abbrev. JSTR) Relatively strong winds concentrated in a narrow stream in the atmosphere, normally referring to horizontal, high-altitude winds. The position and orientation of jet streams vary from day to day. General weather patterns (hot/cold, wet/dry) are related closely to the position, strength and orientation of the jet stream (or jet streams). A jet stream at low levels is known as a low-level jet.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet Wind Speed Profile is: A vertical wind speed profile characterized by a relatively narrow current of high winds with slower moving air above and below. A large wind (speed) shear occurs above and below the jet axis.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jet is: A fast-moving wind current surrounded by slower moving air.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jetty is: In hydrologic terms, a structure (e.g.; a pier, or mole of wood or stone) extending into a sea, lake, or river to influence the current or tide or to protect a harbor
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, JMA is: Japanese Meteorological Agency
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Jokulhlaup is: In hydrologic terms, an Icelandic term meaning glacier dammed lake outburst flood

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, JSTR is: Jet Stream - Relatively strong winds concentrated in a narrow stream in the atmosphere, normally referring to horizontal, high-altitude winds. The position and orientation of jet streams vary from day to day. General weather patterns (hot/cold, wet/dry) are related closely to the position, strength and orientation of the jet stream (or jet streams). A jet stream at low levels is known as a low-level jet.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, JTWC is: Joint Typhoon Warning Center
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Juvenile Water is: In hydrologic terms, water formed chemically within the earth and brought to the surface in intrusive rock

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, K Corona is: In solar-terrestrial terms, of the white-light corona (that is, the corona seen by the eye at a total solar eclipse), that portion which is caused by sunlight scattered by electrons in the hot outer atmosphere of the sun.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, K-Index is: A measure of the thunderstorm potential based on vertical temperature lapse rate, moisture content of the lower atmosphere, and the vertical extent of the moist layer. The temperature difference between 850 mb and 500 mb is used to parameterize the vertical temperature lapse rate. The 850 dew point provides information on the moisture content of the lower atmosphere. The vertical extent of the moist layer is represented by the difference of the 700 mb temperature and 700 mb dew point. This is called the 700 mb temperature-dew point depression. The index is derived arithmetically and does not require a plotted sounding. K-index = (850 mb temperature - 500 mb temperature) + 850 mb dew point - 700 mb dew point depression

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, K is: Smoke- Smoke in various concentrations can cause significant problems for people with respiratory ailments. It becomes a more universal hazard when visibilities are reduced to Â¼ mile or less.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Katabatic Wind is: A wind that is created by air flowing downhill.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Katafront is: A front where the warm air descends the frontal surface (except in the low layers of the atmosphere).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Keetch-Byrum Drought Index is: An index used to gage the severity of drought in deep duff and organic soils.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kelvin-Helmholtz Waves is: Vertical waves in the air associated with wind shear across statically-stable regions. Can appear as breaking waves and as braided patterns in radar images and cloud photos.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kelvin Temperature Scale is: An absolute temperature scale in which a change of 1 Kelvin equals a change of 1 degree Celsius; 0ÂºK is the lowest temperature on the Kelvin scale. The freezing point of water is +273ÂºK (Kelvin) and the boiling point of +373ÂºK. It is used primarily for scientific purposes. It is also known as the Absolute Temperature Scale.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kelvin Waves is: Fluctuations in wind speed at the ocean surface at the Equator result in eastward propagating waves, known as Kelvin Waves. Kelvin Waves cause variations in the depth of the oceanic thermocline, the boundary between warm waters in the upper ocean and cold waters in the deep ocean. They play an important role in monitoring and predicting El NiÃ±o episodes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kilopascal is: The internationally recognized unit used by the Atmospheric Environment Service for measuring atmospheric pressure. Abbreviated kPa.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kinetic Energy is: Energy that a body has as a result of its motion. Mathematically, it is defined as one-half the product of a body's mass and the square of its speed (KE = 1/2 * mass * velocity squared).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Klystron is: An electron tube used as a low-power oscillator or a high-power amplifier at ultrahigh frequencies.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Knot is: (abbrev. Kt) Unit of speed used in navigation, equal to 1 nautical mile (the length of 1 minute latitude) per hour or about 1.15 statute miles per hour, or 0.5 meters/sec).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Knuckles is: Slang for lumpy protrusions on the edges, and sometimes the underside, of a thunderstorm anvil. They usually appear on the upwind side of a back-sheared anvil, and indicate rapid expansion of the anvil due to the presence of a very strong updraft. They are not mammatus clouds. See also cumuliform anvil and anvil rollover.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Kp Index is: A 3-hourly planetary geomagnetic index of activity generated in Gottingen, Germany, based on the K Index from 12 or 13 stations distributed around the world

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, KT is: (Knot)- Unit of speed used in navigation, equal to 1 nautical mile (the length of 1 minute latitude) per hour or about 1.15 statue miles per hour, or 0.5 meters/sec).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, La NiÃ±a is: La NiÃ±a, a phase of ENSO, is a periodic cooling of surface ocean waters in the eastern tropical Pacific along with a shift in convection in the western Pacific further west than the climatological average. These conditions affect weather patterns around the world. The preliminary CPC definition of La NiÃ±a is a phenomenon in the equatorial Pacific Ocean characterized by a negative sea surface temperature departure from normal.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lag is: 1) The measure of the time between the center of mass of precipitation to the center of mass of runoff (on the hydrograph); basin lag is a function of not only basin characteristics, but also of storm intensity and movement. Some hydrologic texts define lag from the center of mass of rainfall to the hydrograph peak. 2) The time it takes a flood wave to move downstream.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Breeze is: A thermally produced wind blowing during the day from the surface of a large lake to the shore, caused by the difference in the rates of heating of the surfaces of the lake and of the land.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Effect Snow Advisory is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when pure lake effect snow (this is where the snow is a direct result of lake effect snow and not because of a low pressure system) may pose a hazard or it is life threatening. The criteria for this advisory varies from area to area.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Effect Snow Squall is: A local, intense, narrow band of moderate to heavy snow squall that can extend long distances inland. It may persist for many hours. It may also be accompanied by strong, gusty, surface winds and possibly lightning. Accumulations can be 6 inches or more in 12 hours.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Effect Snow Warning is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when pure lake effect snow (this is where the snow is a direct result of lake effect snow and not because of a synoptic storm or low pressure system) may pose a hazard or it is life threatening.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Effect Snow is: Snow showers that are created when cold, dry air passes over a large warmer lake, such as one of the Great Lakes, and picks up moisture and heat.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Effect Storm is: A fall or winter storm that produces heavy but localized precipitation as a result of temperature differences between the air over snow-covered ground and the air over the open waters of a lake.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lake Wind Advisory is: This product is issued for sustained wind speeds, generally 20 to 29 mph, lasting for 1 hour or longer for regions which have a significant user community. The need for this product is locally determined.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lakeshore Flood Advisory is: See Coastal/Lakeshore Flood Advisory .
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lakeshore Flood Watch is: See: COASTAL/LAKESHORE FLOOD WATCH
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lakeshore Flooding is: See COASTAL/LAKESHORE FLOODING

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LALs is: (L)ightning (A)ctivity (L)evels. LAL 1 - No thunderstorms. LAL 2 - Few building cumulus with isolated thunderstorms. LAL 3 - Much building cumulus with scattered thunderstorms. Light to moderate rain. LAL 4 - Thunderstorms common. Moderate to heavy rain reaching the ground. LAL 5 - Numerous thunderstorms. Moderate to heavy rain reaching the ground. LAL 6 - Dry lightning (same as LAL 3 but without the rain).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Laminar Flow is: Streamline flow in which successive flow particles follow similar path lines and head loss varies with velocity to the first power.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Laminar is: Smooth, non-turbulent. Often used to describe cloud formations which appear to be shaped by a smooth flow of air traveling in parallel layers or sheets.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Land Breeze is: A coastal breeze at night blowing from land to sea, caused by the difference in the rates of cooling of their respective surfaces.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Landfall is: The intersection of the surface center of a tropical cyclone with a coastline. Because the strongest winds in a tropical cyclone are not located precisely at the center, it is possible for a cyclone's strongest winds to be experienced over land even if landfall does not occur. Similarly, it is possible for a tropical cyclone to make landfall and have its strongest winds remain over the water. Compare direct hit, indirect hit, and strike.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Landspout is: [Slang], a tornado that does not arise from organized storm-scale rotation and therefore is not associated with a wall cloud (visually) or a mesocyclone (on radar). Landspouts typically are observed beneath Cbs or towering cumulus clouds (often as no more than a dust whirl), and essentially are the land-based equivalents of waterspouts.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lapse Rate is: The rate of change of an atmospheric variable, usually temperature, with height. A steep lapse rate implies a rapid decrease in temperature with height (a sign of instability) and a steepening lapse rate implies that destabilization is occurring.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Large Scale is: (Synoptic Scale) Size scale referring generally to weather systems with horizontal dimensions of several hundred miles or more. Most high and low pressure areas seen on weather maps are synoptic-scale systems.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Last Update is: The time and date in which the forecast was issued or updated. The forecast may be updated at any time as weather conditions warrant.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LAT is: Latitude- The location north or south in reference to the equator, which is designated at zero (0) degrees. Lines of latitude are parallel to the equator and circle the globe. The North and South poles are at 90 degrees North and South latitude.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Latent Heat Flux is: The flux of heat from the earth's surface to the atmosphere that is associated with evaporation or condensation of water vapor at the surface; a component of the surface energy budget.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Latent Heat is: Heat absorbed or released during a change of phase at constant temperature and pressure.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Latitude is: (abbrev. LAT) The location north or south in reference to the equator, which is designated at zero (0) degrees. Lines of latitude are parallel to the equator and circle the globe. The North and South poles are at 90 degrees North and South latitude.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LAWEB is: (Great Lakes Weather Broadcast) - A National Weather Service product containing an observation summary prepared to provide Great Lakes mariners with a listing of weather observations along or on the Lakes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Layer Composite Reflectivity Average is: This WSR-88D radar product displays the average reflectivities for a layer. Data is taken from all elevation angles contained in a given layer for each grid box. It is available for 3 layers (low, mid, high). It is used to aid in determining storm intensity trends by comparing mid level layer composite products with a low level elevation angle base reflectivity product and aid in routing air traffic.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Layer Composite Reflectivity Maximum is: This WSR-88D radar product displays the maximum reflectivities for a layer. Data is taken from all elevation angles contained in a given layer for each grid box. It is available for 3 layers (low, mid, high). Currently, the low layer extends from the surface to 24,000 feet, the mid layer extends from 24,000 feet to 33,000 feet, and high layer extends above 33,000 feet. It is used to aid in determining storm intensity trends by comparing mid level layer composite products with a low level elevation angle base reflectivity product and aid in routing air traffic.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Layered Haze is: Haze produced when air pollution from multiple line, area or point sources is transported long distances to form distinguishable layers of discoloration in a stable atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LCD (Local Climatological Data) is: This National Climatic Data Center (NCDC) publication is produced monthly and annually for some 270 United States cities and it's territories. The LCD summarizes temperature, relative humidity, precipitation, cloudiness, wind speed and direction observation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LCL is: 1. Abbreviation for "local" or "locally" 2. Lifting Condensation Level - the level at which a parcel of moist air becomes saturated when it is lifted dry adiabatically.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LDS is: Lightning Detection System
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LDT is: Local Daylight Time.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Leader Spot is: In solar-terrestrial terms, in a magnetically bipolar or multipolar sunspot group, the western part precedes and the main spot in that part is called the leader.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Leader is: The streamer which initiates the first phase of each stroke of a lightning discharge. The first stroke is led by a steeped leader, which may be preceded by a pilot streamer. All subsequent strokes begin with a dart leader.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lee Wave is: The wavelike effect, characterized by severe updrafts and downdrafts, that occurs in the lee of a mountain range when rapidly flowing air is lifted up the steep front of a mountain range. Compare mountain wave.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lee is: The side or part that is sheltered or turned away from the wind, such as with a mountain.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Leeside Low is: Extratropical cyclones that form on the downwind (lee) side of a mountain chain. In the United States, they frequently form on the eastern side of the Rockies and Sierra Nevadas.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Leeward is: The side away from the wind. Compare windward.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Left Exit Region is: Used interchangably with Left Front Quadrant ; the area downstream from and to the left of an upper-level jet max (as would be viewed looking along the direction of flow). Upward motion and severe thunderstorm potential sometimes are increased in this area relative to the wind speed maximum. See also entrance region, right rear quadrant.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Left Front Quadrant is: Used interchangably with Left Exit Region ; the area downstream from and to the left of an upper-level jet max (as would be viewed looking along the direction of flow). Upward motion and severe thunderstorm potential sometimes are increased in this area relative to the wind speed maximum. See also entrance region, right rear quadrant.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Left Mover is: A thunderstorm which moves to the left relative to the steering winds, and to other nearby thunderstorms; often the northern part of a splitting storm.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Length is: In hydrologic terms, the distance in the direction of flow between two specific points along a river, stream, or channel.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lentic System is: In hydrologic terms, a nonflowing or standing body of fresh water, such as a lake or pond

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lenticular Cloud is: A very smooth, round or oval, lens-shaped cloud that is often seen, singly or stacked in groups, near or in the lee of a mountain ridge.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Levee is: (Dike) In hydrologic terms, a long, narrow embankment usually built to protect land from flooding. If built of concrete or masonary the structure is usually referred to as a flood wall. Levees and floodwalls confine streamflow within a specified area to prevent flooding. The term "dike" is used to describe an embankment that blocks an area on a reservoir or lake rim that is lower than the top of the dam.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Level of Free Convection is: (LFC) - The level at which a parcel of saturated air becomes warmer than the surrounding air and begins to rise freely. This occurs most readily in a conditionally unstable atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LEWP is: Line Echo Wave Pattern. A bulge in a thunderstorm line producing a wave-shaped "kink" in the line. The potential for strong outflow and damaging straight-line winds increases near the bulge, which often resembles a bow echo. Severe weather potential also is increased with storms near the crest of a LEWP.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LFC is: An acronym for Level of Free Convection- the level at which a parcel of saturated air becomes warmer than the surrounding air and begins to rise freely. This occurs most readily in a conditionally unstable atmosphere.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LI is: Lifted Index. A common measure of atmospheric instability. Its value is obtained by computing the temperature that air near the ground would have if it were lifted to some higher level (around 18,000 feet, usually) and comparing that temperature to the actual temperature at that level. Negative values indicate instability - the more negative, the more unstable the air is, and the stronger the updrafts are likely to be with any developing thunderstorms. However there are no "magic numbers" or threshold LI values below which severe weather becomes imminent.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lid is: (Also called cap.) A region of negative buoyancy below an existing level of free convection (LFC) where energy must be supplied to the parcel to maintain its ascent. This tends to inhibit the development of convection until some physical mechanism can lift a parcel to its LFC. The intensity of the cap is measured by its convective inhibition. The term capping inversion is sometimes used, but an inversion is not necessary for the conditions producing convective inhibition to exist.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lid is: A layer of warm air several thousand feet above the earth's surface which suppresses or delays the development of thunderstorms.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LIFR is: Low Instrument Flight Rules

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lifted Index is: (abbrev. LI)- A common measure of atmospheric instability. Its value is obtained by computing the temperature that air near the ground would have if it were lifted to some higher level (around 18,000 feet, usually) and comparing that temperature to the actual temperature at that level. Negative values indicate instability - the more negative, the more unstable the air is, and the stronger the updrafts are likely to be with any developing thunderstorms. However there are no "magic numbers" or threshold LI values below which severe weather becomes imminent.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lifting Condensation Level is: (LCL) - The level at which a parcel of moist air becomes saturated when it is lifted dry adiabatically.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Light Bridge is: In solar-terrestrial terms, it is observed in white light, a bright tongue or streaks penetra- ting or crossing sunspot umbrae. The appearance of a light bridge is frequently a sign of impending region division or dissolution

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lightning Channel is: The irregular path through the air along which a lightning discharge occurs. A typical discharge of flash between the ground and the cloud is actually a composite flash which is composed of several sequential lightning strokes, each of which is initiated by a leader and terminated by a return streamer.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lightning Discharge is: The series of electrical processes by which charge is transferred along a channel of high ion density between electrical charge centers of opposite sign. This can be between a cloud and the Earth's surface of a cloud-to-ground discharge.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lightning Stroke is: Any of a series of repeated electrical discharges comprising a single lightning discharge (strike). Specifically, in the case of a cloud-to-ground discharge, a leader plus its subsequent return streamer.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lightning is: (abbrev. LTNG) A visible electrical discharge produced by a thunderstorm. The discharge may occur within or between clouds, between the cloud and air, between a cloud and the ground or between the ground and a cloud.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Likely is: (abbrev. LKLY) In probability of precipitation statements, the equivalent of a 60 or 70 percent chance.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Limb Flare is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a solar flare seen at the edge (Limb) of the sun.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Limb is: In solar-terrestrial terms, the edge of the solar disk.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Limnology is: In hydrologic terms, the branch of hydrology that pertains to the study of lakes

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Line Echo Wave Pattern is: (abbrev. LEWP) A radar echo pattern formed when a segment of a line of thunderstorms surges forward at an accelerated rate.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Line Source is: An array of pollutant sources along a defined path that can be treated in dispersion models as an aggregate uniform release of pollutants along a line. Example: the sum of emissions from individual cars traveling down a highway can be treated as a line source. Compare area source and point source.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Liquid Water Equivalent is: Same as Water Equivalent ; the liquid content of solid precipitation that has accumulated on the ground (snow depth). The accumulation may consist of snow, ice formed by freezing precipitation, freezing liquid precipitation, or ice formed by the refreezing of melted snow.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lithometeor is: Atmospheric phenomena which affect the state of the atmosphere. They constitute dry particles that hang suspended in the atmosphere, such as dust, smoke, sand, and haze.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lithosphere is: In hydrologic terms, that part of the earth which is composed predominantly of rocks (either coherent or incoherent, and including the disintegrated rock materials known as soils and subsoils), together with everything in this rocky crust.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Littoral Zone is: In hydrologic terms, the area on, or near the shore of a body water

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Live Capacity is: In hydrologic terms, the total amount of storage capacity available in a reservoir for all purposes, from the dead storage level to the normal water or normal pool level surface level. Does not include surcharge, or dead storage, but does include inactive storage, active conservation storage and exclusive flood control storage.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LIVV is: Lifted Index Vertical Velocity
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LKLY is: Likely- In probability of precipitation statements, the equivalent of a 60 or 70 percent chance.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LLJ is: Low Level Jet - A region of relatively strong winds in the lower part of the atmosphere. Specifically, it often refers to a southerly wind maximum in the boundary layer, common over the Plains states at night during the warm season (spring and summer). The term also may be used to describe a narrow zone of strong winds above the boundary layer, but in this sense the more proper term would be low-level jet stream.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LLWS is: Low Level Wind Shear

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Loaded Gun (Sounding) is: [Slang], a sounding characterized by extreme instability but containing a cap, such that explosive thunderstorm development can be expected if the cap can be weakened or the air below it heated sufficiently to overcome it.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Local Convective Wind is: In fire weather terminology, local thermally driven winds arising over a comparatively small area and influenced by local terrain. Examples include sea and land breezes, lake breezes, diurnal mountain wind systems and columnar convective currents.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lock & Dam (L&D) is: Used in navigable rivers, lock and dams allow for large ships to move from one level of water to another.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lofting is: A pattern of plume dispersion in a stable boundary layer topped by a neutral layer, in which the upper part of the plume disperses upward while the lower part of the plume undergoes little dispersion.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Long Term Retention is: Retention of data for 5 years to satisfy requirements for local studies and to support litigation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Longitude is: The location east or west in reference to the Prime Meridian, which is designated as zero (0) degrees longitude. The distance between lines of longitude are greater at the equator and smaller at the higher latitudes, intersecting at the earth's North and South Poles. Time zones are correlated to longitude.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Longwave Radiation is: A term used to describe the infrared energy emitted by the earth and atmosphere at wavelengths between about 5 and 25 micrometers. Compare shortwave radiation.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Longwave Trough is: A trough in the prevailing westerly flow aloft which is characterized by large length and (usually) long duration.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Loop Prominence System is: (abbrev. LPS) In solar-terrestrial terms, a system of loop prominences associated with major flares.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Looping is: A pattern of plume dispersion in an unstable atmosphere, in which the plume undergoes marked vertical oscillations as it is alternately affected by rising convective plumes and the subsiding motions between the plumes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LORAN is: Long Range Navigation, a system of long range navigation whereby latitude and longitude are determined from the time displacement of radio signals from two or more fixed transmitters.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lotic System is: In hydrologic terms, a flowing body of fresh water, such as a river or stream.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Low Frequency is: (abbrev. LF) The portion of the radio frequency spectrum from 30 to 300 kHz.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Low Level Jet is: (abbrev. LLJ)- A region of relatively strong winds in the lower part of the atmosphere. Specifically, it often refers to a southerly wind maximum in the boundary layer, common over the Plains states at night during the warm season (spring and summer). The term also may be used to describe a narrow zone of strong winds above the boundary layer, but in this sense the more proper term would be low-level jet stream.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Low Pressure System is: An area of a relative pressure minimum that has converging winds and rotates in the same direction as the earth. This is counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Also known as an cyclone, it is the opposite of an area of high pressure, or a anticyclone.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Low Water Advisory is: An advisory to describe water levels which are significantly below average levels over the Great Lakes, coastal marine zones, and any tidal marine area, waterway, or river inlet within or adjacent to a marine zone that would potentially be impacted by low water conditions creating a hazard to navigation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Low is: A region of low pressure, marked as "L" on a weather map. A low center is usually accompanied by precipitation, extensive cloudiness, and moderate winds. See Cyclone.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lowland Flooding is: In hydrologic terms, inundation of low areas near the river, often rural, but may also occur in urban areas.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LP Storm is: Low-Precipitation storm (or Low-Precipitation supercell). A supercell thunderstorm characterized by a relative lack of visible precipitation. Visually similar to a classic supercell, except without the heavy precipitation core. LP storms often exhibit a striking visual appearance; the main tower often is bell-shaped, with a corkscrew appearance suggesting rotation. They are capable of producing tornadoes and very large hail. Radar identification often is difficult relative to other types of supercells, so visual reports are very important. LP storms almost always occur on or near the dry line, and thus are sometimes referred to as dry line storms.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LPS is: Loop Prominence System- In solar-terrestrial terms, a system of loop prominences associated with major flares.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LSR is: Local Storm Report. A product issued by local NWS offices to inform users of reports of severe and/or significant weather-related events

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, LTNG is: Lightning- A visible electrical discharge produced by a thunderstorm. The discharge may occur within or between clouds, between the cloud and air, between a cloud and the ground or between the ground and a cloud.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Lysimeter is: In hydrologic terms, a device to measure the quantity or rate of downward water movement through a block of soil usually undisturbed, or to collect such percolated water for analysis as to quality

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, M 3000 is: In solar-terrestrial terms, the optimum high frequency radio wave with a 3000 km range, which reflects only once from the ionosphere (single hop transmission)
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, M2/S2 is: m 2 /s 2 (meters squared per second squared), unit of measure equivalent to J/kg (joules per kilogram).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Mackeral Sky is: The name given to cirrocumulus clouds with small vertical extent and composed of ice crystals. The rippled effect gives the appearance of fish scales.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Macroburst is: A convective downdraft with an affected outflow area of at least 2Â½ miles wide and peak winds lasting between 5 and 20 minutes. Intense macrobursts may cause tornado-force damage of up to F3 intensity.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Macroscale is: Large scale, characteristic of weather systems several hundred to several thousand kilometers in diameter.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Madden-Julian Oscillation is: (abbrev. MJO)- Tropical rainfall exhibits strong variability on time scales shorter than the seasonal El NiÃ±o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). These fluctuations in tropical rainfall often go through an entire cycle in 30-60 days, and are referred to as the Madden-Julian Oscillation or intraseasonal oscillations. The intraseasonal oscillations are a naturally occurring component of our coupled ocean-atmosphere system. They significantly affect the atmospheric circulation throughout the global Tropics and subtropics, and also strongly affect the wintertime jet stream and atmospheric circulation features over the North Pacific and western North America.
