High 7 - 9 15 - 24 min. Apply SPF 15 to 30, wear a hat and sunglasses. Limit midday exposure. Very High 10+ 10 min. Apply SPF 30; wear a hat, sunglasses, and protective clothing; limit midday exposure.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, UVM is: Upward Vertical Motion (also known as Upward Vertical Velocity)
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, UVV is: Upward Vertical Velocity (rising air)

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, V Notch is: A radar reflectivity signature seen as a V-shaped notch in the downwind part of a thunderstorm echo. The V-notch often is seen on supercells, and is thought to be a sign of diverging flow around the main storm updraft (and hence a very strong updraft). This term should not be confused with inflow notch or with enhanced V, although the latter is believed to form by a similar process.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VAAC is: Volcanic Ash Advisory Centers

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VAD Wind Profile is: A radar plot of horizontal winds, derived from VAD data, as a function of height above a Doppler Radar. The display is plotted with height as the vertical axis and time as the horizontal axis (a so-called time-height display), which then depicts the change in wind with time at various heights. This display is useful for observing local changes in vertical wind shear, such as backing of low-level winds, increases in speed shear, and development or evolution of nearby jet streams (including low-level jets). This product often is referred to erroneously as a VAD.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VAD is: Velocity Azimuth Display

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vadose Zone is: The locus of points just above the water table where soil pores may either contain air or water. This is also called the zone of aeration

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VALDRIFT is: An air pollution transport and diffusion model developed to determine pesticide drift from aerial spraying operations in valleys.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Valid Time Event Code is: (VTEC) - The Valid Time Event Code (VTEC) always is used in conjunction with, and provides supplementary information to, the Universal Geographic Code (UGC), to further aid in the automated delivery of National Weather Service text products to users. The VTEC is included in many event driven or non-routine products and in some routine Marine forecasts. The VTEC provides information on the event, while the UGC describes the affected geographic area.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Valid Time is: The period of time during which a forecast or warning, until it is updated or superseded by a new forecast issuance, is in effect.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Valley Exit Jet is: A strong elevated down-valley air current issuing from a valley above its intersection with the adjacent plain.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Valley Volume Effect is: The reduction in volume of a valley (or basin) as compared to an equal depth volume with a horizontal floor. Because the valley volume is smaller, equivalent heat fluxes will cause larger changes in temperature in the valley volume than in the flat-floor volume.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Valve is: In hydrologic terms, a device fitted to a pipeline or orifice in which the closure member is either rotated or moved in some way as to control or stop flow.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vapor Pressure is: The partial pressure of water vapor in an air-water system.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) is: A large-scale, semi-distributed hydrologic model that solves full water and energy balances. As such, it shares several basic features with other land surface models that are commonly coupled to global circulation models.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Variable Wind Direction is: A condition when (1) the wind direction fluctuates by 60Â° or more during the 2-minute evaluation period and the wind speed is greater than 6 knots; or (2) the direction is variable and the wind speed is less than 6 knots.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Variable Wind is: Same as Variable Wind Direction ; a condition when (1) the wind direction fluctuates by 60Â° or more during the 2-minute evaluation period and the wind speed is greater than 6 knots; or (2) the direction is variable and the wind speed is less than 6 knots.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Variance is: A measure of variability.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VCP is: Volume Coverage Pattern - A volumetric sampling procedure designed for the surveillance of one or more particular meteorological phenomena. Clear Air Mode uses VCP 31 and 32. Each has a Volume Scan consisting of 5 elevation angles (0.5 to 4.5 degrees) in ten minutes. VCP 31 has a long pulse length and provides a better signal-to-noise ratio permitting lower reflectivity returns to be detected. VCP 32 has a short pulse length which provides for larger unambiguous velocity values. Precipitation Mode uses VCP 11 and 21. VCP 11 provides better vertical sampling of weather echoes near the antenna and is usually preferred in situations where convective precipitation is within 60 nmi of the antenna. VCP 11 Volume Scan consists of 14 elevation angles (0.5 to 19.5 degrees) in 5 minutes. VCP 21 has a slower antenna rotation rate and provides better velocity and spectrum width estimates beyond 60 nmi. VCP 21 Volume Scan consists of 9 elevation angles (0.5 to 19.5 degrees) in 6 minutes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Veering Winds is: Winds which shift in a clockwise direction with time at a given location (e.g., from southerly to westerly), or which change direction in a clockwise sense with height (e.g., southeasterly at the surface turning to southwesterly aloft). The latter example is a form of directional shear which is important for tornado formation. Compare with backing winds.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Veering is: A clockwise shift in wind direction (for example, south winds shifting to the west).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Velocity Azimuth Display is: A WSR 88-D product which shows the radar derived wind speeds at various heights. This radar product shows the wind speeds from 2,000 to 55,000 feet above the ground. VAD and EVAD (Extended VAD) are methods of guessing the large scale two-dimensional winds from one-dimensional radial velocity data. They are essentially multivariate regressions which fit a simple, large scale wind model to the observed winds. EVAD also estimates the large scale horizontal divergence and particle fall speed. See VWP.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Velocity Cross Section is: This WSR-88D radar product displays a vertical cross section of velocity on a grid with heights up to 70,000 feet on the vertical axis and distance up to 124 nm on the horizontal axis. The two end points to create cross section are radar operator selected along a radial or from one AZRAN to another AZRAN within 124 nm of the radar that are less than 124 nm apart. It is used to: 1) Examine storm structure features such as location of updrafts/downdrafts, strength of storm top divergence, and the depth of mesocyclones; 2) Locate areas of convergence/divergence (when generated along a radial; and 3) Analyze areas of rotation (when generated from one AZRAN to another).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Velocity Zones is: In hydrologic terms, areas within the floodplain subject to potential high damage from waves. These sometimes appear on flood insurance rate maps

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ventilation Index is: Product of the mixing depth and transport wind speed, a measure of the potential of the atmosphere to disperse airborne pollutants from a stationary source. Sometimes referred to as a Clearing Index.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Venturi Effect is: The speedup of air through a constriction due to the pressure rise on the upwind side of the constriction and the pressure drop on the downwind side as the air diverges to leave the constriction.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Ver High Frequency (VHF) is: That portion of the radio frequency spectrum from 30 to 300 MHz

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vertical Velocity is: The component of velocity (motion) in the vertical. The evaluation of areas of upward vertical velocity is key to forecasting areas of active weather.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vertical Wind Shear is: the change in the wind's direction and speed with height. This is a critical factor in determining whether severe thunderstorms will develop.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vertically Stacked System is: A low-pressure system, usually a closed low or cutoff low, which is not tilted with height, i.e., located similarly at all levels of the atmosphere. Such systems typically are weakening and are slow-moving, and are less likely to produce severe weather than tilted systems. However, cold pools aloft associated with vertically-stacked systems may enhance instability enough to produce severe weather.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Very Low Frequency (VLF) is: That portion of the radio frequency spectrum from 3 to 30 kHz

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VIL is: Vertically-Integrated Liquid water. A property computed by RADAP II and WSR-88D units that takes into account the three-dimensional reflectivity of an echo. The maximum VIL of a storm is useful in determining its potential severity, especially in terms of maximum hail size.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VIP is: Video Integrator and Processor, which contours radar reflectivity (in dBZ) into six VIP levels: VIP 1 (Level 1, 18-30 dBZ) - Light precipitation. VIP 2 (Level 2, 30-38 dBZ) - Light to moderate rain. VIP 3 (Level 3, 38-44 dBZ) - Moderate to heavy rain. VIP 4 (Level 4, 44-50 dBZ) - Heavy rain. VIP 5 (Level 5, 50-57 dBZ) - Very heavy rain; hail possible. VIP 6 (Level 6, >57 dBZ) - Very heavy rain and hail; large hail possible.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Virga is: Streaks or wisps of precipitation falling from a cloud but evaporating before reaching the ground. In certain cases, shafts of virga may precede a microburst.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Virtual Potential Temperature is: The virtual potential temperature is the temperature a parcel at a specific pressure level and virtual temperature would have if it were lowered or raised to 1000 mb. This is defined by Poisson's equation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Virtual Temperature is: The virtual temperature is the temperature a parcel which contains no moisture would have to equal the density of a parcel at a specific temperature and humidity.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VIS is: 1. Visible satellite imagery 2. Visibile or Visibility

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Visibility Protection Program is: The program specified by the Clean Air Act to achieve a national goal of remedying existing impairments to visibility and preventing future visibility impairment throughout the United States.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Visibility is: The distance at which a given standard object can be seen and identified with the unaided eye
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Visible Infra-Red Imaging Radiometer (VIIRS) is: A medium-resolution sensor flown aboard the NOAA-20 and Suomi-NP satellites.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Visible Satellite Imagery is: This type of satellite imagery uses reflected sunlight (this is actually reflected solar radiation) to see things in the atmosphere and on the Earth's surface. Clouds and fresh snow are excellent reflectors, so they appear white on the imagery. Clouds can be distinguished from snow, because clouds move and snow does not move. Meanwhile, the ground reflects less sunlight, so it appears black on the imagery. The satellite uses its 0.55 to 0.75 micrometer (um) channel to detect this reflected sunlight. Since this imagery relies on reflected imagery, it cannot be used during night.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Visual Spectrum is: The portion of the electromagnetic spectrum to which the eye is sensitive, i.e., light with wavelengths between 0.4 and 0.7 micrometers. Compare shortwave radiation and longwave radiation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VMD is: Volume median diameter. A statistical measure of the average droplet size in a spray cloud, such that fifty percent of the volume of sprayed material is composed of droplets smaller in diameter than the VMD.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vog is: Vog, short for volcanic smog, is the haze formed by gas and fine particle emissions from volcanoes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Volcanic Ash is: Fine particles of mineral matter from a volcanic eruption which can be dispersed long distances by winds aloft. The chemical composition and abrasiveness of the particles can seriously affect aircraft and also machinery on the ground. If it is blown into the stratosphere and it is thick enough, it can decrease the global temperature.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Volume Scan is: A radar scanning strategy in which sweeps are made at successive antenna elevations (i.e., a tilt sequence), and then combined to obtain the three-dimensional structure of the echoes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Volume Velocity Processing is: A way to guess the large-scale 2-dimensional winds, divergence and fall speeds from one-dimensional radial velocity data. Essentially a multivariate regression which fits a simple wind model to the observed radial velocities. Very similar to VAD and EVAD, except it uses different functions for the fit.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Voluntary Observing Ship Program is: (VOS) - An international voluntary marine observation program under the auspices of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Observations are coded in a special format known as the ships synoptic code, or "BBXX" format. They are then distributed for use by meteorologists in weather forecasting, by oceanographers, ship routing services, fishermen, and many others.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vort Max is: Common slang reference to Vorticity Maximum ; a center, or maximum, in the vorticity field of a fluid.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vortex is: A whirling mass of air in the form of a column or spiral. It need not be oriented vertically but, for example, could be rotating around a horizontal axis.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Vorticity is: A measure of the rotation of air in a horizontal plane. Positive (counter-clockwise or cyclonic) vorticity can be correlated with surface low development and upward vertical motion (in areas of positive vorticity advection).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VOS is: (Voluntary Observing Ship Program) - An international voluntary marine observation program under the auspices of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Observations are coded in a special format known as the ships synoptic code, or "BBXX" format. They are then distributed for use by meteorologists in weather forecasting, by oceanographers, ship routing services, fishermen, and many others.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VSB is: Visible Satellite Imagery

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VTEC is: (Valid Time Event Code) - The Valid Time Event Code (VTEC) always is used in conjunction with, and provides supplementary information to, the Universal Geographic Code (UGC), to further aid in the automated delivery of National Weather Service text products to users. The VTEC is included in many event driven or non-routine products and in some routine Marine forecasts. The VTEC provides information on the event, while the UGC describes the affected geographic area.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VVP is: Volume Velocity Processing - a way to guess the large-scale 2-dimensional winds, divergence and fall speeds from one-dimensional radial velocity data. Essentially a multivariate regression which fits a simple wind model to the observed radial velocities. Very similar to VAD and EVAD, except it uses different functions for the fit.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VVSTORM is: Model-based convection algorithm.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, VWP is: VAD Wind Profile - a radar plot of horizontal winds, derived from VAD data, as a function of height above a Doppler Radar. The display is plotted with height as the vertical axis and time as the horizontal axis (a so-called time-height display), which then depicts the change in wind with time at various heights. This display is useful for observing local changes in vertical wind shear, such as backing of low-level winds, increases in speed shear, and development or evolution of nearby jet streams (including low-level jets). This product often is referred to erroneously as a VAD.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WAA is: Warm Air Advection - the advection (movement) of warm air into a region.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wake is: The region of turbulence immediately to the rear of a solid body caused by the flow of air over or around the body.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wall Cloud is: A localized, persistent, often abrupt lowering from a rain-free base. Wall clouds can range from a fraction of a mile up to nearly five miles in diameter, and normally are found on the south or southwest (inflow) side of the thunderstorm. When seen from within several miles, many wall clouds exhibit rapid upward motion and cyclonic rotation. However, not all wall clouds rotate. Rotating wall clouds usually develop before strong or violent tornadoes, by anywhere from a few minutes up to nearly an hour. Wall clouds should be monitored visually for signs of persistent, sustained rotation and/or rapid vertical motion. "Wall cloud" also is used occasionally in tropical meteorology to describe the inner cloud wall surrounding the eye of a tropical cyclone, but the proper term for this feature is eyewall.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warm Advection is: Transport of warm air into an area by horizontal winds. Low-level warm advection sometimes is referred to (erroneously) as overrunning. Although the two terms are not properly interchangeable, both imply the presence of lifting in low levels.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warm Core Low is: A low pressure area which is warmer at its center than at its periphery. Tropical cyclones exhibit this temperature pattern. Unlike cold core lows, these lows produce much of their cloud cover and precipitation during the nighttime.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warm Front is: A transition zone between a mass of warm air and the colder air it is replacing.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warm Occlusion is: A frontal zone formed when a cold front overtakes a warm front and, finding colder air ahead of the warm front, leaves the ground and rises up and over this denser air. Compare with cold occlusion.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warm Sector is: A region of warm surface air between a cold front and a warm front.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Warning is: A warning is issued when a hazardous weather or hydrologic event is occurring, is imminent, or has a very high probability of occurring. A warning is used for conditions posing a threat to life or property.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wasatch Wind is: A strong easterly wind blowing out of the mouths of the canyons of the Wasatch Mountains onto the plains of Utah. Also called canyon wind.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watch Box is: (or simply "Box") - slang for a Severe Thunderstorm Watch or Tornado Watch issued by the SPC.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watch Cancellation is: This product will be issued to let the public know when either a Tornado Watch or Severe Thunderstorm Watch has been canceled early. It is issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) in Norman, Oklahoma. In the text of the statement it will specify the severe weather watch number and the area which the watch covered.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watch Redefining Statement is: This product tells the public which counties/parishes are included in the watch. This is done not only by writing them all out, but by using the county FIPS codes in the Header of the product. It is issued by the local National Weather Service Forecast Office (WFO).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watch Status Reports is: This product lets the NWFO know of the status of the current severe weather watch (Tornado or Severe Thunderstorm). During the severe weather watch, the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) will issue these reports periodically. These reports will describe, in plain language, the current evaluation of the severe weather situation and whether the watch will expire or be reissued. A status report is not issued if a cancellation or replacement has been issued at least 1 hour prior to the expiration time of the original watch.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watch is: A watch is used when the risk of a hazardous weather or hydrologic event has increased significantly, but its occurrence, location, and/or timing is still uncertain. It is intended to provide enough lead time so that those who need to set their plans in motion can do so.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Equivalent is: The liquid content of solid precipitation that has accumulated on the ground (snow depth). The accumulation may consist of snow, ice formed by freezing precipitation, freezing liquid precipitation, or ice formed by the refreezing of melted snow.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Pollution is: The alteration of the constituents of a body of water by man to such a degree that the water loses its value as a natural resource.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Supply Outlook is: A seasonal volume forecast, generally for a period centered around the time of spring snowmelt (e.g., April-July). The outlooks are in units of acre-feet and represent the expected volume of water to pass by a given point during a snowmelt season. The outlook categories include Most Probable, Reasonable Maximum, and Reasonable Minimum.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Table is: The level below the earth's surface at which the ground becomes saturated with water. The water table is set where hydrostatic pressure equals atmospheric pressure.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Vapor Plume is: This appears in the water vapor satellite imagery. It is a plume-like object that extends from the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) northward or southward into the higher latitudes. It is usually located over a 850 to 700 mb theta-e ridge axis. As a result, it is a favored location for the development of a Mesoscale Convective Complex (MCC). Researchers have found it to be a favored region for very heavy rain. It is thought that the ice crystals located in this plume help thunderstorms to become highly efficient rainfall producers. In North America, this is sometimes called the "Mexican Connection".
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Water Year is: The time period from October 1 through September 30.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watercourse is: Any surface flow such as a river, stream, tributary.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watershed is: Land area from which water drains toward a common watercourse in a natural basin.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Waterspout is: In general, a tornado occurring over water. Specifically, it normally refers to a small, relatively weak rotating column of air over water beneath a Cb or towering cumulus cloud. Waterspouts are most common over tropical or subtropical waters. The exact definition of waterspout is debatable. In most cases the term is reserved for small vortices over water that are not associated with storm-scale rotation (i.e., they are the water-based equivalent of landspouts). But there is sufficient justification for calling virtually any rotating column of air a waterspout if it is in contact with a water surface.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Watt is: Unit of power in the MKS system of units; energy per unit of time, one Joule per second (1 J/s). Abbreviated W.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Crest is: The highest part of a wave
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Height is: Distance from wave trough to wave crest.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Period is: Time, in seconds, between the passage of consecutive wave crests past a fixed point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Spectrum is: The distribution of wave energy with respect to wave frequency or period. Wave spectra assist in differentiating between wind waves and swell.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Steepness is: The ratio of wave height to wavelength and is an indicator of wave stability. When wave steepness exceeds a 1/7 ratio; the wave typically becomes unstable and begins to break.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wave Trough is: The lowest part of the wave.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wavelength is: Distance between crests or troughs of a wave.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WAVEWATCH III is: One of the operational forecast models run at NCEP. The WWIII is run four times daily, with forecast output out to 126 hours.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WBZ is: Wet Bulb Zero - the height where the wet-bulb temperature goes below 0Â°C. It is important because WBZ heights between 7000 ft and 10,500 ft (above ground level) correlate well with large hail at the surface when storms develop in an airmass primed for strong convection. Higher values infer mid and upper level stability and also indicate a large melting area for falling hail. Lower WBZ heights indicate that the low level atmosphere is often too cool and stable to support large hail.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WC/ATWC is: West Coast and Alaska Tsunami Warning Center. The National Weather Service's West Coast and Alaska Tsunami Warning Center in Palmer, AK has a regional tsunami responsibility for the Canadian coastal regions and the ocean coasts of all U.S. States except Hawaii. See also PTWC.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WCM is: Warning Coordination Meteorologist

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WDIR is: On a buoy report, wind direction (the direction the wind is coming from in degrees clockwise from true N) during the same period used for WSPD.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Weak Echo Region is: (Abbrev. WER) - A WSR-88D radar product which displays reflectivity for up to 8 elevation angles for a radar operator selected location as a set presentation of a storm. The plains in this product are presented in an ascending order, lowest plain is lowest elevation angle selected. It is used to depict storm tilt and to identify Weak Echo Regions (WER) and Bounded Weak Echo Regions (BWER) in thunderstorms.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Weather Forecast Office is: (Abbrev. WFO) - this type of National Weather Service office is responsible for issuing advisories, warnings, statements, and short term forecasts for its county warning area

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Weather is: The state of the atmosphere with respect to wind, temperature, cloudiness, moisture, pressure, etc. Weather refers to these conditions at a given point in time (e.g., today's high temperature), whereas Climate refers to the "average" weather conditions for an area over a long period of time (e.g., the average high temperature for today's date).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wedge Tornado is: Slang for a large tornado with a condensation funnel that is at least as wide (horizontally) at the ground as it is tall (vertically) from the ground to cloud base. The term "wedge" often is used somewhat loosely to describe any large tornado. However, not every large tornado is a wedge. A true wedge tornado, with a funnel at least as wide at the ground as it is tall, is very rare. Wedges often appear with violent tornadoes (F4 or F5 on the Fujita Scale), but many documented wedges have been rated lower. And some violent tornadoes may not appear as wedges (e.g., Xenia, OH on 3 April 1974, which was rated F5 but appeared only as a series of suction vortices without a central condensation funnel). Whether or not a tornado achieves "wedge" status depends on several factors other than intensity - in particular, the height of the environmental cloud base and the availability of moisture below cloud base. Therefore, spotters should not estimate wind speeds or F-scale ratings based on visual appearance alone. However, it generally is safe to assume that most (if not all) wedges have the potential to produce strong (F2/F3) or violent (F4/F5) damage.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WEFAX is: System for transmitting weather charts and imagery via satellite. Occasionally used as an abbreviation for radiofacsimile via HF radio.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Weighing-Type Precipitation Gage is: A rain gage that weighs the rain or snow which falls into a bucket set on a platform of a spring or lever balance. The increasing weight of its contents plus the bucket are recorded on a chart. The record thus shows the accumulation of precipitation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Weir is: In hydrologic terms, (a) A low dam built across a stream to raise the upstream water level (fixed-crest weir when uncontrolled); (b) A structure built across a stream or channel for the purpose of measuring flow (measuring or gaging weir).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WER is: Weak Echo Region - Radar term for a region of relatively weak reflectivity at low levels on the inflow side of a thunderstorm echo, topped by stronger reflectivity in the form of an echo overhang directly above it. The WER is a sign of a strong updraft on the inflow side of a storm, within which precipitation is held aloft. When the area of low reflectivity extends upward into, and is surrounded by, the higher reflectivity aloft, it becomes a BWER.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, West African Disturbance Line is: A line of convection about 300 miles long, similar to a squall line. It forms over west Africa north of the equator and south of 15 degrees North latitude. It moves faster than an Easterly Wave between 20 and 40 mph. They move off the African coast every 4 to 5 days mainly in the summer. Some reach the American tropics and a few develop into tropical cyclones.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, West Wall is: The coast side boundary of the Gulf Stream, typically south of Cape Hatteras. See also North Wall
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Westerlies is: The prevailing winds that blow from the west in the mid-latitudes.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wet Bulb Globe Temperature is: An indication of expected heat stress on humans taking into account temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and cloud cover (solar radiation).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wet-Bulb Temperature is: The lowest temperature that can be obtained by evaporting water into the air.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wet Bulb Zero is: (Abbrev. WBZ) - the height where the wet-bulb temperature goes below 0Â°C. It is important because WBZ heights between 7000 ft and 10,500 ft (above ground level) correlate well with large hail at the surface when storms develop in an airmass primed for strong convection. Higher values infer mid and upper level stability and also indicate a large melting area for falling hail. Lower WBZ heights indicate that the low level atmosphere is often too cool and stable to support large hail.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wet Floodproofing is: In hydrologic terms, an approach to floodproofing which usually is a last resort. Flood waters are intentionally allowed into the building to minimize water pressure on the structure. Wet Floodproofing can include moving a few valueable items to a higher place or completely rebuilding the floodable area. Wet floodproofing has an advantage over other approaches: no matter how little is done, flood damage will be reduced. Thousands of dollars in damage can be avoided just by moving furniture and appliances out of the flood-prone area.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wet Microburst is: A microburst accompanied by heavy precipitation at the surface. A rain foot may be a visible sign of a wet microburst.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wetland is: In hydrologic terms, an area that is regularly wet or flooded and has a water table that stands at or above the land surface for at least part of the year.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WFO is: Weather Forecast Office - this type of National Weather Service office is responsible for issuing advisories, warnings, statements, and short term forecasts for its county warning area
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Whirlwind is: A small, rotating column of air; may be visible as a dust devil.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, White Light Flare is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a major flare in which small parts become visible in white light. Such flares are usually strong X-ray, radio, and particle emitters.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, White Light (WL) is: Sunlight integrated over the visible portion of the spectrum (4000 - 7000 angstroms) so that all colors are blended to appear white to the eye.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Whitecap is: The breaking crest of a wave, usually white and frothy.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Widespread is: Areal coverage of non-measurable, non-convective weather and/or restrictions to visibility affecting more than 50 percent of a forecast zone(s).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wildfire is: Any free burning uncontainable wildland fire not prescribed for the area which consumes the natural fuels and spreads in response to its environment.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wildlands is: Any nonurbanized land not under extensive agricultural cultivation, e.g., forests, grasslands, rangelands.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Willy-Willy is: In Australia, a dust devil. Also formerly used to denote a tropical cyclone.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Advisory is: This product is issued for strong winds that are not expected to reach warning criteria. Generally for sustained wind speeds of 30 to 39 mph lasting for 1 hour or longer.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Chill is: A measure of how cold people and animals feel when outside. Wind chill is based on the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold. As a general rule, the threshold for potentially dangerous wind chill conditions is about -20°F and lower.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Couplet is: An area on the radar display where two maximum wind speeds are blowing in opposite directions.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Direction is: The true direction from which the wind is blowing at a given location (i.e., wind blowing from the north to the south is a north wind). It is normally measured in tens of degrees from 10 degrees clockwise through 360 degrees. North is 360 degrees. A wind direction of 0 degrees is only used when wind is calm.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Field is: The three-dimensional spatial pattern of winds.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Gust is: Rapid fluctuations in the wind speed with a variation of 10 knots or more between peaks and lulls. The speed of the gust will be the maximum instantaneous wind speed.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Radii is: Term used in National Weather Tropical Cyclone Forecast Advisory products (TCM). Wind radii are the largest radii of that wind speed found in that quadrant. Quadrants are defined as NE (0-90), SE (90-180), SW (180-270), and NW (270-0). As an example, given maximum 34 knot radii to 150 nm at 0 degrees, 90 at 120 degrees, and 40 nm at 260 degrees, the following line would be carried in the forecast/advisory: 150NE 90SE 40SW 150NW.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Rose is: A diagram, for a given locality or area, showing the frequency and strength of the wind from various directions.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Shear Profile is: The change in wind speed and/or direction usually in the vertical. The characteristics of the wind shear profile are of critical importance in determining the potential for and type of severe weather.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Shear is: The rate at which wind velocity changes from point to point in a given direction (as, vertically). The shear can be speed shear (where speed changes between the two points, but not direction), direction shear (where direction changes between the two points, but not speed) or a combination of the two.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Shift Line is: A long, but narrow axis across which the winds change direction (usually veer).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Shift is: A change in wind direction of 45 degrees or more in less than 15 minutes with sustained wind speeds of 10 knots or more throughout the wind shift.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Sock is: A tapered fabric shaped like a cone that indicates wind direction by pointing away from the wind. It is also called a "wind cone."

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Speed is: The rate at which air is moving horizontally past a given point. It may be a 2-minute average speed (reported as wind speed) or an instantaneous speed (reported as a peak wind speed, wind gust, or squall).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind Waves is: Local, short period waves generated from the action of wind on the water surface (as opposed to swell). Commonly referred to as waves. In a National Weather Service Coastal Marine Forecast or Offshore Forecast, wind waves are used when swells are described in the forecast. or Waves generated by the local wind blowing at the time of observation.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wind is: The horizontal motion of the air past a given point. Winds begin with differences in air pressures. Pressure that's higher at one place than another sets up a force pushing from the high toward the low pressure. The greater the difference in pressures, the stronger the force. The distance between the area of high pressure and the area of low pressure also determines how fast the moving air is accelerated. Meteorologists refer to the force that starts the wind flowing as the "pressure gradient force." High and low pressure are relative. There's no set number that divides high and low pressure. Wind is used to describe the prevailing direction from which the wind is blowing with the speed given usually in miles per hour or knots.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Windward is: The side toward the wind. Compare with leeward.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter Pool is: The pool, or height of the water surface, of a reservoir during the winter. This pool is usually a specific height and is maintained for the control of late winter and spring flooding.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter Solstice is: The time at which the sun is farthest south in the Southern Hemisphere, on or around December 21.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter Storm Warning is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when a winter storm is producing or is forecast to produce heavy snow or significant ice accumulations. The criteria for this warning can vary from place to place.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter Storm Watch is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when there is a potential for heavy snow or significant ice accumulations, usually at least 24 to 36 hours in advance. The criteria for this watch can vary from place to place.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter Weather Advisory is: This product is issued by the National Weather Service when a low pressure system produces a combination of winter weather (snow, freezing rain, sleet, etc.) that present a hazard, but does not meet warning criteria.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Winter is: Typically the coldest season of the year during which the sun is farthest from overhead. In the Northern Hemisphere, winter customarily includes the months of December, January and February.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wire Weight Gage is: In hydrologic terms, a river gage comprised of a weight which is lowered to the water level. The weight is attached to a cable; and as the weight is lowered, a counter indicates the length of cable released. The stage is determined from the length of cable required to reach the water level.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WMC is: World Meteorological Center(s)
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WMO is: World Meteorological Organization (UN)

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wolf Number is: A historic term for Sunspot Number. In 1849, R. Wolf of Zurich originated the general procedure for computing the sunspot number

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Wrapping Gust Front is: A gust front which wraps around a mesocyclone, cutting off the inflow of warm moist air to the mesocyclone circulation and resulting in an occluded mesocyclone.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WRCC is: Western Regional Climate Center
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSFO is: Weather Service Forecast Office

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSPD is: On a buoy report, the wind speed (m/s) averaged over an eight-minute period for buoys and a two-minute period for land stations. Reported Hourly.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSR-57 is: A NWS Weather Surveillance Radar designed in 1957. It used to be part of weather radar network. It was replaced by WSR-88D units.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSR-74 is: A NWS Weather Surveillance Radar designed in 1974. It used to be part of weather radar network. It was replaced by WSR-88D units.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSR-88D System is: The summation of all hardware, software, facilities, communications, logistics, staffing, training, operations, and procedures specifically associated with the collection, processing, analysis, dissemination and application of data from the WSR-88D unit.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSR-88D is: Weather Surveillance Radar - 1988 Doppler; NEXRAD unit.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WSW is: Winter Storm Message
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WTMP is: On a buoy report, the sea surface temperature (Celsius).
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WV is: 1. Water Vapor (satellite imagery) 2. Wave 3. West Virginia

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WVHT is: On a buoy report, significant wave height (meters) is calculated as the average of the highest one-third of all of the wave heights during the 20-minute sampling period.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WW is: Severe Thunderstorm or Tornado Watch

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WWH is: On a buoy report, Wind Wave Height is the vertical distance (meters) between any wind wave crest and the succeeding wind wave trough (independent of swell waves).

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WWP is: On a buoy report, Wind Wave Period is the time (in seconds) that it takes successive wind wave crests or troughs to pass a fixed point.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WWV is: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) radio stations which broadcast a time and frequency service commonly known to mariners as the "Time Tick", used as an aid in celestial navigation. Included in these are hourly voice broadcasts of current warnings for the Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf of Mexico provided by the National Weather Service.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, WWVH is: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) radio stations which broadcast a time and frequency service commonly known to mariners as the "Time Tick", used as an aid in celestial navigation. Included in these are hourly voice broadcasts of current warnings for the Atlantic, Pacific and Gulf of Mexico provided by the National Weather Service.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, X-Band is: A frequency band of microwave radiation in which radars operate.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, X-Ray Background is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a daily average background X-ray flux in the 1 to 8 angstrom range. It is a midday minimum designed to reduce the effects of flares.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, X-Ray Burst is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a temporary enhancement of the X-ray emission of the sun. The time-intensity profile of soft X-ray bursts is similar to that of the H-alpha profile of an associated flare.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, X-Ray Flare Class is: In solar-terrestrial terms, rank of a flare based on its X-ray energy output. Flares are classified by the order of magnitude of the peak burst intensity (I) measured at the earth in the 1 to 8 angstrom band as follows: Class Intensity (in Watts/m 2 ) B I -6 C 10 -6 -5 M 10 -5 -4 X I >= 10 -4

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, X-Rays is: Very energetic electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths intermediate between 0.01 and 10 nanometers (0.1-100 Angstroms) or between gamma rays and ultraviolet radiation. Essentially all X-Rays from space are absorbed in the Earth's upper atmosphere.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, XBT is: Expendable Bathythermograph
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Year is: The period during which the Earth completes one revolution around the sun.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Yellow Snow is: Snow given a golden or yellow appearance by the presence in it of pine, cypress pollen, or anthropogenic material or animal-produced material.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Z\/R Relationship is: An empirical relationship between radar reflectivity factor z (in mm^6 / m^3 ) and rain rate ( in mm / hr ), usually expressed as Z = A R^b; A and b are empirical constants.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Z is: Zulu time; the same as Universal Coordinated Time (UTC), i.e. 18z is the same as 18:00 UTC.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zero Datum is: In hydrologic terms, a reference "zero" elevation for a stream or river gage. This "zero" can be referenced (usually within ten feet of the bottom of the channel) to mean sea level, or to any other recognized datum.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, ZFP is: Zone Forecast Product

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zonal Flow is: Large-scale atmospheric flow in which the east-west component (i.e., latitudinal) is dominant. The accompanying meridional (north-south) component often is weaker than normal. Compare with meridional flow.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zone of Aeration is: In hydrologic terms, the locus of points just above the water table where soil pores may either contain air or water. This is also called the vadose zone

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zone of Saturation is: In hydrologic terms, the locus of points below the water table where soil pores are filled with water. This is also called the phreatic zone

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zoned Embankment Dam is: In hydrologic terms, an embankment dam which is comprised of zones of selected materials having different degrees of porosity, permeability and density.

In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zulu (Z) Time is: For practical purposes, the same as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The notation formerly used to identify time Greenwich MeanTime. The word "Zulu" is notation in the phonetic alphabet corresponding to the letter "Z" assigned to the time zone on the Greenwich Prime Meridian.
In meteorology as defined by the U.S. National Weather Service, Zurich Sunspot Classification is: In solar-terrestrial terms, a sunspot classification system that has been modified for SESC use.
The National Weather Service publishes a list of alert types for its public warning products; the first entry in that list is 911 Telephone Outage.
notes: Maintained by the update engine. Reports what the agency publishes, not which hazards exist.

The Beaufort wind force scale relates wind speed to observable effects on the sea surface and on land, which allows an estimate without an anemometer.
The Beaufort wind force scale is numbered from force 0, described as calm, to force 12, described as hurricane force.
The Enhanced Fujita Scale rates tornado intensity from EF0 to EF5 by estimating wind speed from observed damage, rather than by direct wind measurement.
On the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, a Category 1 hurricane has one-minute sustained winds of 74 to 95 miles per hour.
On the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, a Category 5 hurricane has one-minute sustained winds of 157 miles per hour or higher.
The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale classifies hurricanes by sustained wind speed alone and does not account for storm surge, rainfall or flooding.
